abstract: |
  Children's tendency to generalize new words by shape, the shape bias, is well documented in English-speaking children and reportedly weaker in children acquiring typologically different languages such as Korean. A prominent explanation, the statistical generalization account, attributes the bias to the distributional dominance of shape-organized nouns in the early lexicon. Across English and  Korean adult rating samples, most early nouns were rated as solid and countable, but far fewer were organized by shape than the account predicts, and we detected no differences in shape ratings across the English-rated unilemma sets of 16 languages. Yet, mean shape ratings predicted earlier age of acquisition. Furthermore, Korean adults rated more nouns as shape-organized than English adults, the opposite of the developmental pattern reported in word extension tasks with Korean children. Because adult ratings judge the learned lexicon rather than children's perceptual input, we read these results as constraining the lexical-statistics version of the account such that in its simplest form, it does not by itself explain cross-linguistic variation in the shape bias. Across 4 studies, we find a consistent dissociation in the lexical statistics adults attribute to early nouns: shape is a good cue for early noun learning rather than a common one.

table_panel <- function(df, caption, label, note = NULL, align = NULL,
                        escape = TRUE, stub_indents = NULL) {
  prep <- df
  if (!is.null(stub_indents)) {
    prep <- as.data.frame(prep, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    prep <- papaja:::indent_stubs(prep, stub_indents)
  }
  prep <- papaja:::format_cells(prep, list(digits = 2))
  if (escape) {
    prep <- as.data.frame(lapply(prep, papaja:::escape_latex, spaces = TRUE),
                          check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    caption <- papaja:::escape_latex(caption)
    if (!is.null(note)) note <- papaja:::escape_latex(note)
  }
  if (is.null(align)) {
    align <- paste0("l", strrep("r", max(0L, ncol(prep) - 1L)))
  }
  inner <- papaja:::apa_table_latex(
    x = prep, caption = caption, note = note, placement = "",
    escape = FALSE, align = align, booktabs = TRUE, label = NA
  )
  inner <- paste(inner, collapse = "\n")
  inner <- gsub("\\\\label\\{tab:[^}]+\\}", "", inner)
  inner <- sub("(\\\\caption\\{)", paste0("\\1\\\\label{tab:", label, "}"), inner)
  inner <- gsub("\\\\begin\\{table\\}\\s*", "", inner)
  inner <- gsub("\\\\end\\{table\\}\\s*", "", inner)
  inner <- gsub("\\\\begin\\{center\\}\\s*", "", inner)
  inner <- gsub("\\\\end\\{center\\}\\s*", "", inner)
  inner <- gsub("\\\\normalsize\\{", "\\\\tiny{", inner)
  paste0(
    "\\centering\n\\tiny\n",
    inner
  )
}

emit_table_pair <- function(left, right) {
  # One float holding two side-by-side table panels; pairs are emitted at
  # separate points in the text so each lands near its first reference.
  paste(
    c(
      "\\begin{table}[!htbp]",
      "\\centering",
      "\\captionsetup{font=tiny,skip=1pt,labelfont=tiny,textfont=tiny}",
      "\\begin{minipage}[t]{0.48\\textwidth}",
      left,
      "\\end{minipage}\\hfill",
      "\\begin{minipage}[t]{0.48\\textwidth}",
      right,
      "\\end{minipage}",
      "\\end{table}"
    ),
    collapse = "\n"
  )
}

       fills = list(fill = euler_fills, alpha = 0.55),

       main = list(label = title, fontsize = 9))
}

# Introduction

The shape bias is the tendency of young children to generalize new words to new category members based on their shape [@landau1988] rather than other perceptual attributes like color, texture, or size [@landau1988; @subrahmanyam_2006] or conceptual attributes like a functional, thematic, or a taxonomic match [@imai_childrens_1994; @Poulin-Dubois1999; @imai2010; @yoshida2003known].  Researchers’ long-standing interest in the shape bias relates to its hypothesized role in early word learning. This bias has been extensively studied in English-speaking children in the US, where it emerges early and is thought to be a key mechanism for rapid vocabulary growth after the second year [@gershkoff-stowe_shape_2004; @smith_object_2002]. 

One prominent explanation of the shape bias is that it is a statistical generalization of the early lexicon composition. The reasoning for this explanation is that solid objects that are referred to by count nouns are dominant in the early English lexicon [@samuelson1999]. These objects are usually organized by shape ("the category of balls are all ball shaped, while the category of water does not have a specific shape"). Several lines of evidence support this statistical generalization perspective on the shape bias. For example, when 17-month-olds were trained on names of objects that shared the exact same shape, but different in all their other dimensions, they developed a second order shape bias, and they showed more rapid acquisition of nouns as measured by parental reports [@smith_object_2002]. Training on close similarity of shape, and the consistency in the input is thought to be driving the bias and helped vocabulary acceleration. On the other hand, @Perry2010_Variability found that variability of the exemplars of the category, for example different shapes of a "chair" instead of the exact same shape, predicts higher rate of acquisition. Nevertheless, both studies linked a higher order shape bias generalization to vocabulary growth. We refer to this account as the “statistical generalization” hypothesis.

The shape bias is thought to emerge developmentally during the period in which, on average, these distributional regularities become prominent in young children's early vocabulary. For example, @samuelson1999 asked 26 English-speaking adults in the US to judge the 312 nouns of the toddler MB-CDI, the parental-report measure of the productive vocabulary of children between 16 and 30 months; 13 adults judged count-mass syntax, and the other 13 judged solidity and category organization. Using an 85% agreement criterion (11 of 13 judges), 232 nouns (74%) were classified as count nouns, 197 (63%) as referring to solid things, and 150 (48%) as naming categories organized by shape similarity, with 110 nouns in the intersection of all three. Thus, perhaps when children learn the shape bias, they are learning about this cluster of properties and how much they co-vary.

The statistical generalization hypothesis is also supported by computational models showing that exposure to a lexicon with similar statistical properties can lead to the emergence of a shape bias in simulated learners [@colunga_smith_2005; @perry_samuelson_2011]. A study utilizing Bayesian models further demonstrated that the shape bias can emerge from the statistical structure of the lexicon [@kemp_learning_2007], although this schematic model did not engage the precise statistics of the English lexicon.

## Cross-linguistic variation 

The statistical generalization hypothesis makes a key prediction: in languages with different distributional structures, the resulting inductive bias should be different. In particular, if the strength of the shape bias or even its presence depends on the degree of correspondence between the distributional properties of environmental (i.e. the dominance of solid vs. non-solid objects, artifacts vs. natural objects, or shape organization of categories) and linguistic correlates (i.e. count or mass syntax, classifiers) of nouns to object kinds mapping, then cross-linguistic variation in these correlates should predict cross-linguistic variation in the shape bias. For example, the shape bias has been found to be weaker in children acquiring East Asian languages such as Korean and Japanese [@gathercole_1997; @imai1997; @imai_2008; @yoshida_smith_2005; @Abdelrahim_Frank_2026].

One aspect, the syntactic distinction between count and mass nouns, is a fundamental aspect of noun classification in many languages. Count nouns typically refer to discrete, countable objects (e.g., "dog", "car"), while mass nouns refer to uncountable substances or aggregates (e.g., "water", "sand"). In English, count nouns are often associated with solid objects that are organized by shape, while mass nouns are more likely to refer to non-solid substances that are organized by material [@barner_snedeker_2005; @bloom_1994]. This syntactic distinction is thought to play a crucial role in the development of the shape bias, as children learn to associate count nouns with shape-based categorization and mass nouns with material-based categorization [@samuelson1999; @smith_naming_1996]. The mechanism by which syntax operates has been debated: syntax may permanently change the mental construal of the referent, or it may act as a temporary cue that children accumulate across time and correlate with additional cues that guide their attention to shape as a relevant feature for categorization.

Some studies have suggested that the shape bias may be less pronounced or absent in languages with different noun classification systems or morphological structures (e.g., Chinese, Japanese, Korean). The lack of this distinctive linguistic cue that differentiates between count and mass nouns and the corresponding referents make the correlates that give rise to the shape bias less salient in some languages. For example, in languages like Korean and Japanese, where the count-mass distinction is not as syntactically marked as in English, children may be less likely to develop a strong shape bias. 

## The current study

We ask whether the relevant lexical statistics for the emergence of the shape bias are in fact dominant, vary across languages in line with the child shape bias, and predict when individual words are learned. An ideal test would require independent, precise measurements of both the lexical statistics for a set of languages and the shape bias estimates of groups of children acquiring those languages. This study design is cost-prohibitive, however. Thus, as an initial step, we used a combination of pre-existing data and new annotations to examine differences in lexical statistics across early-learned nouns in 16 languages.

Following the general design of @samuelson1999, in Study 1 we asked English-speaking raters to judge lexical properties of early learned nouns in the chosen languages. Using pre-existing cross-linguistic conceptual mappings "uni-lemmas", we then map these ratings to the early vocabularies of children acquiring these different languages. These ratings then create a proxy for the cluster of noun concepts being learned by children speaking these languages. This strategy has the weakness that cross-linguistic differences may not emerge due to the source of the ratings for all languages being English speakers. If there are conceptual differences that lead to differences in lexical properties for the same item across languages and cultures, then homogeneous ratings would mask those differences. To address this issue, in Study 2 we compare ratings from Korean speakers, an East Asian language that is thought to have a weaker shape bias. In Study 3 we manipulate response format and semantic grouping factorially and identify which factors move the ratings.

We test three predictions of the statistical generalization account, plus one methodological question that the cross-linguistic comparison raises and that must be settled before the predictions can be evaluated:

1. We first collect English-speaker ratings to isolate the lexicon-side prediction.

2. If the conceptions are universal, English- and Korean-speaker ratings of the same items should align; if they diverge, that divergence is itself a cross-linguistic signal that the unilemma-based design in Study 1 is unable to detect.

3. The statistical-generalization account makes the further prediction that the lexical properties dominant in early vocabulary should also be the ones that predict when individual words are acquired. We use externally derived age of acquisition (AoA) estimates to model AoA, and ask whether shape, solidity, and countability uniquely predict AoA after controlling for word frequency and concreteness. A dissociation between which features are common in the early lexicon and which features predict early acquisition would distinguish a "good-cue" account (shape facilitates learning when it is available) from a pure "exposure" account (shape facilitates learning because it is dominant in the input).

shape_prop_per_item <- function(df, item_col = "word") {
  df %>%
    filter(block == "category_organization") %>%
    distinct(.data[[item_col]], matching_response, proportion) %>%
    group_by(.data[[item_col]]) %>%
    summarise(
      shape_prop = proportion[matching_response == "shape"][1],
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(shape_prop = replace_na(shape_prop, 0))
}
```

# Split-half (random rater halves, Spearman-Brown) reliability of the
# item-level proportions per block. The organizing block necessarily uses
# identifier-present trials only (see the missing-identifier footnote).
split_half_sb <- function(df, target_resp, n_rep = 100) {
  df <- df %>% dplyr::filter(!is.na(subject))
  rs <- replicate(n_rep, {
    d <- df %>% dplyr::group_by(word) %>%
      dplyr::mutate(h = sample(rep_len(c(1, 2), dplyr::n()))) %>%
      dplyr::ungroup()
    w <- d %>% dplyr::group_by(word, h) %>%
      dplyr::summarise(p = mean(response == target_resp), n = dplyr::n(),
                       .groups = "drop") %>%
      tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = h, values_from = c(p, n)) %>%
      dplyr::filter(!is.na(p_1), !is.na(p_2), n_1 >= 2, n_2 >= 2)
    cor(w$p_1, w$p_2)
  })
  r <- mean(rs)
  round(2 * r / (1 + r), 2)
}
set.seed(7)

sb_count_1a <- split_half_sb(english_sample1_raw %>%
                               dplyr::filter(block == "count_mass"), "count noun")
sb_shape_1a <- split_half_sb(english_sample1_raw %>%
                               dplyr::filter(block == "category_organization"), "shape")

# Conditional structure: shape among the nouns that satisfy the antecedent
# of the overhypothesis (>= 80% solid and >= 80% count).
word_scc <- english_sample1 %>%
  dplyr::filter(matching_response %in% c("solid", "count")) %>%
  dplyr::distinct(word, matching_response, proportion) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = matching_response, values_from = proportion,
                     values_fill = 0) %>%
  dplyr::left_join(s1a_shape, by = "word")
cond80        <- word_scc %>% dplyr::filter(solid >= 0.8, count >= 0.8)
n_cond80      <- nrow(cond80)
m_cond80      <- round(mean(cond80$shape_prop), 2)
pct_cond80_80 <- round(100 * mean(cond80$shape_prop >= 0.8))

# Scale-fair statistics for the four-option organizing block: response
# shares over all trials, and the modal response per item, which do not
# depend on the number of response alternatives.
org_counts_1a <- english_sample1 %>%
  dplyr::filter(block == "category_organization") %>%
  dplyr::distinct(word, matching_response, count)
org_share_1a <- org_counts_1a %>%
  dplyr::group_by(matching_response) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(k = sum(count), .groups = "drop") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(share = k / sum(k))
osh_1a <- function(r) sprintf("%.0f",
  100 * org_share_1a$share[org_share_1a$matching_response == r])
committed_shape_1a <- sprintf("%.0f", 100 *
  org_share_1a$k[org_share_1a$matching_response == "shape"] /
  sum(org_share_1a$k[org_share_1a$matching_response %in%
                       c("shape", "color", "material")]))
modal_pct_1a <- function(bl, target) {
  d <- english_sample1 %>% dplyr::filter(block == bl) %>%
    dplyr::distinct(word, response, count)
  m <- d %>% dplyr::group_by(word) %>%
    dplyr::slice_max(count, n = 1, with_ties = TRUE) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(nt = dplyr::n()) %>% dplyr::ungroup() %>%
    dplyr::filter(nt == 1)
  sprintf("%.0f", 100 * sum(m$response == target) / dplyr::n_distinct(d$word))
}
```

## Methods

This study extends @samuelson1999 by collecting ratings on early learned nouns from the CDI of 16 languages including English. The ratings were collected for the same three dimensions, but for a much larger set of nouns (N = `r n_unique_uni`) that are early learned across these 16 languages. We then compared the distribution of ratings across languages, and the correspondence between the three dimensions across languages.

### Participants

`r n_part_1a` English-speaking adults recruited online from the Prolific platform (mean age = 41, SD = 14) were asked to rate nouns on three dimensions: solidity (solid, non-solid, unclear), count and mass noun syntax (count, mass, unclear), and organizing feature (shape, color, material, none of these).^[A session-logging error left the participant identifier missing on `r pct_na_subj_1a`% of retained trials, in a  pseudo-randomly sampled category-organization block to balance item coverage. Those trials are included in the item-level proportions. A sensitivity analysis in the supplementary materials with the unattributed trials excluded left the results unchanged] All participants provided informed consent prior to participation.

### Materials

A set of nouns were sourced from CDI data on the Wordbank repository of 16 languages ("English (American)", "Mandarin (Beijing)", "Korean", "English (Australian)", "Cantonese", "Catalan" , "Japanese", "Turkish" , "Spanish (Mexican)", "Russian", "Kiswahili", "Mandarin (Taiwanese)", "Spanish (Peruvian)", "Spanish (European)", "Hebrew", "French (French)") that represented seven linguistic families: (Indo-European, Sino-Tibetan, Koreanic, Japonic, Turkic, Niger-Congo, Afro-Asiatic), and were available through the Wordbank software package. 
The nouns were chosen based on the earliest age of acquisition in the dataset, up to a maximum of 300 nouns. Because we only recruited English-speaking participants, nouns were presented in English and mapped across languages via conceptual mappings, universal lemmas or “unilemmas” [@frank2021variability]. A “unilemma” is the concept behind the noun expressed in the English language (“dog” and “Hund” both map to the same underlying concept of “dog”, which is used as the unilemma in this case). 

Across the `r n_lang_rated` languages, the early-noun lists comprised `r prettyNum(n_noun_entries, big.mark = ",")` noun-by-language entries. Because many concepts recur across languages, these reduce to `r n_unique_uni` unique unilemmas after removing duplicates, which is the set English raters judged. The pairwise overlap between the languages is quantified in the supplementary materials, along with the breakdown of the semantic categories. Most nouns belonged to the semantic categories of food and drinks, clothing, and animals, with a few words referring to vehicles, toys, body parts, household items, and outside things. The size of the noun set for each language differs based on the availability of data in the Wordbank repository (M = `r perlang_mean`, min = `r perlang_min`, max = `r perlang_max`, SD = `r perlang_sd` nouns per language). 

### Procedure

The experiment started with familiarization trials in which participants were provided with demonstrations of count and mass nouns, solid objects, and non-solid objects. They were also familiarized with what a category-organizing or characterizing feature means (The organizing feature for pottery is the material used, while for ball is shape of the object for example). Then the test trials followed the same wording and structure. Every dimension (solidity, count-mass syntax, and category organizing feature) constituted a block, and every participant rated 20 nouns per block, so there were 60 test trials per participant in total. Familiarization trials, test blocks, and nouns within a block were all randomized across participants. No information about the semantic category of nouns was given to participants, nor were the nouns grouped by their semantic category. Participants were only allowed to choose one feature in all questions. Full trial wording and interface are documented with browser-ready experiment files in the public repository.

```{r trial-schematic, include=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
# ggplot schematic omitted from main PDF; identical logic lives in repo `experiment files/`
# (solidity-ratings.*, vocab_comp.*). Knit chunk retained if you want to regenerate locally.
# Test-trial wording matches jsPsych SurveyMultiChoice prompts in solidity-ratings.js (1A)
# and vocab_comp.js (2A): lemma-only prompts for solidity/count_mass; category prompt uses
# timeline lemma + "belongs to a category that is organized by:" with four options.
ex_word <- "apple"
trial_panels <- tibble::tibble(
  block = factor(
    c("Solidity", "Count-mass syntax", "Organizing feature"),
    levels = c("Solidity", "Count-mass syntax", "Organizing feature")
  ),
  prompt = c(
    paste0(ex_word, "\n(word presented alone as prompt)"),
    paste0(ex_word, "\n(word presented alone as prompt)"),
    paste0(ex_word, " belongs to a category\nthat is organized by:")
  ),
  options = c(
    "solid · non-solid · unclear/unknown",
    "count noun · mass noun · unclear/unknown",
    "shape · color · material · none of these"
  )
)

ggplot(trial_panels, aes(x = 0.5, y = 1)) +
  geom_rect(xmin = 0, xmax = 1, ymin = 0, ymax = 1,
            fill = "white", color = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(y = 0.82, label = paste0("Block: ", block)),
            size = 3.5, fontface = "bold") +
  geom_text(aes(y = 0.54, label = prompt), size = 3.15, lineheight = 1.05) +
  geom_text(aes(y = 0.22, label = paste0("Responses: ", options)),
            size = 2.95, fontface = "italic", color = "grey25") +
  facet_wrap(~ block, nrow = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(strip.text = element_blank(),
        panel.spacing = unit(0.55, "lines"))
```

### Data analysis
```{r correspondenceeng1-prep, include=FALSE}
representative_langs <- c("English (American)", "Korean",
                          "Mandarin (Beijing)", "Japanese")

correspondence_eng1_main <- english_sample1 %>%
  filter(matching_response %in% c("solid", "count", "shape"),
         language %in% representative_langs)
```

```{r correspondenceeng1, include=TRUE, fig.cap="Word-level rating distributions for solid, count, and shape responses in four representative languages from Study 1 (English American, Korean, Mandarin Beijing, Japanese). Curves show kernel density of per-word proportions; the 12 remaining languages appear in the Supplement.", fig.align = "center", fig.pos = "H", out.width = "70%"}
ggplot(correspondence_eng1_main,
       aes(x = proportion, color = response, fill = response)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ language, ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "Proportion of trials", y = "Density (words)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

We calculated the proportion of responses for each feature per noun. For example, if a word was rated by 10 participants in total, and 7 of them rated it as solid, the proportion of solid responses for that word would be 0.7. First, we assessed the correspondence between the three dimensions using Pearson correlation analysis. We then conducted a permutation test by shuffling language labels, comparing each language's distribution of shape-based categorization responses against a null distribution of no cross-linguistic differences. Because the bands are pointwise rather than simultaneous, an observed curve that stays within the envelope indicates an absence of detectable differences rather than a demonstration of equivalence. 

Additionally, and similar to @samuelson1999, who classified nouns using an 85% agreement criterion and report similar conclusions under a 60% sensitivity criterion, we categorized the nouns into three categories: solid, count noun, and shape-based using a cutoff of 80%, a slightly less conservative value. A noun rated by at least 80% of the participants as solid is categorized as solid, and likewise for the other dimensions. We then visualized the overlap between these categories using Euler diagrams.

Lastly, we also calculated inter-rater agreement using the word-level consensus approach, which involves calculating the mode of the ratings for each word and then computing the percentage of raters who agreed with the mode. This gives us a measure of how consistently participants rated each word across the three dimensions.

#Venn Diagram

threshold <- 0.8

category_english_sample1 <- english_sample1 |>
  filter(response %in% c("solid", "count noun")) |>
  mutate(over_threshold = proportion >= threshold) |>
  select(uni_lemma, language, word, response, over_threshold) |>

              aes(x = x, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
              fill = "darkgrey", alpha = 0.5) +

            aes(x = x, y = density),
            color = "blue", size = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ language) +
  labs(x = "Proportion of 'shape' choices", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal() +

        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),

        axis.text = element_text(size = 7))
```

We collected ratings from `r n_part_1a` participants across the three blocks. After dropping practice and attention-check trials and trials with no recorded response, `r prettyNum(n_ratings_1a, big.mark = ",")` ratings were retained for analysis, covering `r n_items_1a` nouns (per-block noun counts differ by a few nouns because not every noun retained ratings in every block, which is why item counts vary slightly across analyses). Nouns received an average of `r abr("solidity")` (solidity), `r abr("count_mass")` (count-mass), and `r abr("category_organization")` (category-organizing) ratings per block. Included in the supplementary materials are the demographic details of the participants and the distribution of ratings across nouns and blocks.

Word-level inter-rater agreement, computed as the proportion of raters choosing the modal response for each noun and then averaged across nouns, was high for solidity (`r con_e1("solidity")`) and count-mass syntax (`r con_e1("count_mass")`), and lower but well above chance for the organizing-feature block (`r con_e1("category_organization")`), the dimension raters found hardest to articulate. Split-half reliabilities of the item-level proportions (random rater halves, Spearman-Brown corrected, 100 splits) show the same ordering: `r sb_solid_1a` for solidity, `r sb_count_1a` for count-mass syntax, and `r sb_shape_1a` for the organizing feature within this sample alone. This leaves substantial item-level noise that could by itself produce a flat or low shape distribution, and the analyses that build on this measure therefore use item-level proportions averaged across two independent samples. The retest reported below provides a second, test-retest check on the shape measure.

Across languages, the ratings proportions were very consistent, suggesting limited variation in the distributional statistics (Figure \@ref(fig:correspondenceeng1)); Figure \@ref(fig:permutateddisteng1) shows the formal comparison of each language's shape distribution against a permuted-label null envelope. Overall, nouns "uni-lemmas" were predominantly rated as solid (M = `r m_e1("solid")`, SD = `r sd_e1("solid")`) and count (M = `r m_e1("count")`, SD = `r sd_e1("count")`), but were less reliably judged as being organized by shape (M = `r m_e1("shape")`, SD = `r sd_e1("shape")`). Raters spread organizing-feature responses over material (`r osh_1a("material")`%), none of these (`r osh_1a("none of these")`%), shape (`r osh_1a("shape")`%), and color (`r osh_1a("color")`%), so shape accounted for `r committed_shape_1a`% of committed (shape, color, or material) responses. At the item level, the modal organizing feature was material for `r modal_pct_1a("category_organization", "material")`% of nouns, shape for `r modal_pct_1a("category_organization", "shape")`%, and none of these for `r modal_pct_1a("category_organization", "none of these")`%, whereas the modal response was solid for `r modal_pct_1a("solidity", "solid")`% of nouns and count for `r modal_pct_1a("count_mass", "count noun")`%. There was a moderate positive correlation between solidity and count syntax ($r$ = `r r_e1("count noun", "solid")`, `r fmt_p(p_e1("count noun", "solid"))`), a weak positive correlation between count syntax and shape-based categorization ($r$ = `r r_e1("count noun", "shape")`, `r fmt_p(p_e1("count noun", "shape"))`), and a weaker positive correlation between solidity and shape-based categorization ($r$ = `r r_e1("solid", "shape")`, `r fmt_p(p_e1("solid", "shape"))`). Conditional on the `r n_cond80` nouns meeting the 80% criterion for both solidity and count syntax, mean shape rose only to `r m_cond80`, and `r pct_cond80_80`% met the 80% shape criterion, a much sparser intersection than the 110 of 312 nouns @samuelson1999 reported at their 85% criterion.

The Euler diagram in Figure \@ref(fig:venneng1) shows categories of nouns as solid, count noun, and shape-characterized using the 80% cutoff. The diagram shows that a large number of nouns were consistently rated as solid and count nouns, with large overlap between these two dimensions. However, at most `r max_shape_venn_eng1` nouns per language were rated as referring to objects organized by shape. For comparison, @samuelson1999 classified 150 of their 312 nouns (48%) as naming shape-organized categories under their 85% agreement criterion, with 110 nouns in the intersection of solid, count, and shape.

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\centering
\captionsetup{font=tiny,skip=1pt,labelfont=tiny,textfont=tiny}
\includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{data/figures/venneng1.png}
\caption{Area-proportional Euler diagrams of the overlap between nouns categorized as solid, count, and shape-organized in four representative languages from Study 1. A noun is assigned to a category when at least 80\% of raters chose that response; circle areas are proportional to set sizes (fitted layout near-exact, diagError $<$ 0.01). The full 16-language version appears in the Supplement.}
\label{fig:venneng1}
\end{figure}

The permutation test for distributional differences results showed that each set of nouns fell within the null distribution, indicating no significant differences in lexical statistics across languages as rated by English speakers (Figure \ref{fig:permutateddisteng1}).

## Retest ratings for lexical properties

One concern is measurement reliability rather than cross-linguistic patterning. The notion of an "organizing feature" is not one that adults routinely articulate, and our initial instructions were minimal. The low shape-based choices, large standard deviation, and weak shape–solidity correlation could partly reflect measurement error. We address this by re-running the category-organizing-feature block with refined instructions. The idea of the organizing feature of an object category is not an intuitive one, and is not something that people actively think about when recognizing category members i.e. when they are searching for apples, they don't break down the category into features of apple shape, red color, and leaf material and then decide which feature is the most diagnosing of apples. It is possible that the instructions were not clear enough for participants to understand what was being asked. To test the reliability of this measure, we collected a second sample of ratings on the same set of words, with improved instructions and examples. 
```{r }
english_sample2 <- read_csv(here("data/predictors","english_sample2_props.csv"))
english_sample2 <- english_sample2 %>% filter(!is.na(response)) %>% distinct()
english_sample2_raw <- read_csv(here("data/predictors","english_sample2_raw.csv"))

english_sample2$response_numeric <- mapply(map_categories, english_sample2$response, english_sample2$block)
```

```{r s1b-pool-check}
# The Study 1B stimulus list did not fully coincide with the Study 1A list:
# it lacked 40 of the 664 Study 1A nouns (they appear nowhere in the raw
# Study 1B trials) and contained other nouns not analyzed here. Compare the
# absent nouns to the covered ones on the Study 1A measures.
w1b_pool <- unique(english_sample2_raw$theword[!is.na(english_sample2_raw$theword)])
miss_1b  <- setdiff(unique(english_sample1$word), w1b_pool)
props_1a_cmp <- english_sample1 %>%
  dplyr::filter(matching_response %in% c("solid", "count")) %>%
  dplyr::distinct(word, matching_response, proportion) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = matching_response,
                     values_from = proportion, values_fill = 0) %>%
  dplyr::left_join(shape_prop_per_item(english_sample1, "word"), by = "word") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(miss1b = word %in% miss_1b)
tt_miss_shape <- t.test(shape_prop ~ miss1b, data = props_1a_cmp)
m_miss <- function(v, g) round(mean(props_1a_cmp[[v]][props_1a_cmp$miss1b == g],
                                    na.rm = TRUE), 2)
```

```{r }
english_sample2 |>
  filter(block == "category_organization") |>
ggplot(aes(x = proportion, color = response, fill = response)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ language) +
  labs(
    title = "Density of Proportions by Language",

```{r}
eng_samp1_shape <- shape_prop_per_item(english_sample1, "word") %>%
  rename(proportion = shape_prop)
eng_samp2_shape <- shape_prop_per_item(english_sample2, "word") %>%
  rename(proportion = shape_prop)

merged_data <- merge(eng_samp1_shape, eng_samp2_shape, by = "word",
                     suffixes = c(".sample1", ".sample2")) %>% distinct()

correlation_score <- cor(merged_data$proportion.sample1, merged_data$proportion.sample2, use = "complete.obs") # Handles missing values

print(paste("correlation between shape proportions in 1A VS 1B is: ", correlation_score))

#using the spearman-brown prediction formula 
predicted_reliability <- (2 * correlation_score) / (1 + correlation_score)
print(paste("predicted reliability using spearman-brown formula is: ", predicted_reliability))

# Conditional (overhypothesis) analysis from Study 1A, recomputed on the
# two-sample averaged shape measure (nouns absent from 1B keep the 1A value).
cond80_avg <- cond80 %>%
  dplyr::left_join(eng_samp2_shape %>% dplyr::rename(s2 = proportion),
                   by = "word") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(avg_shape = ifelse(is.na(s2), shape_prop,
                                   (shape_prop + s2) / 2))
m_cond80_avg   <- round(mean(cond80_avg$avg_shape), 2)
pct_cond80_avg <- round(100 * mean(cond80_avg$avg_shape >= 0.8), 1)
```

```{r }
study1a_shape_tbl <- shape_prop_per_item(english_sample1, "word") %>%
  left_join(english_sample1 %>% distinct(word, uni_lemma, language),
            by = "word")
study1b_shape_tbl <- shape_prop_per_item(english_sample2, "word") %>%
  left_join(english_sample2 %>% distinct(word, uni_lemma, language),
            by = "word")

study1a_data <- study1a_shape_tbl %>%
  transmute(uni_lemma, language, shape_rating = shape_prop, study = "1A")
study1b_data <- study1b_shape_tbl %>%
  transmute(uni_lemma, language, shape_rating = shape_prop, study = "1B")

combined_data <- bind_rows( 
  study1b_data, study1a_data
   ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(shape_rating)) %>%  # Remove missing values
mutate(shape_rating = as.numeric(shape_rating)) %>%
  distinct()  # Remove duplicates

# wide format for reliability
ratings_wide <- combined_data %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = study, 
              values_from = shape_rating,
              names_prefix = "Study_") %>%
  filter(!is.na(Study_1A) & !is.na(Study_1B))  # Only words rated in both studies

ratings_wide_distinct <- ratings_wide %>% distinct(uni_lemma, .keep_all = TRUE)

overall_reliability<- cor.test(ratings_wide_distinct$Study_1A, 
                               ratings_wide_distinct$Study_1B, 
                               use = "complete.obs")

descriptive_stats <- combined_data %>%
  group_by(study) %>%
  summarise(
    n_ratings = n(),
    n_words = n_distinct(uni_lemma),
    mean_rating = mean(shape_rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_rating = sd(shape_rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_rating = median(shape_rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    q25 = quantile(shape_rating, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    q75 = quantile(shape_rating, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

```

```{r }
# Mixed-effects model comparing studies
comparison_model <- lmer(shape_rating ~ study + 
                        (1 | uni_lemma) + 
                        (1 | language),
                        data = combined_data)
eng_cmp_coefs <- coef(summary(comparison_model))
eng_cmp_B <- eng_cmp_coefs["study1B", "Estimate"]
eng_cmp_p <- eng_cmp_coefs["study1B", "Pr(>|t|)"]
```

#### Participants

`r dplyr::n_distinct(english_sample2_raw$subject)` English-speaking adults recruited online from the Prolific platform rated words on the category-organizing feature.

#### Materials

Only the category-organizing feature block was included in this retest, since it showed the most between subject variability. The retest word list was generated separately with `r length(miss_1b)` of the `r dplyr::n_distinct(english_sample1$word)` Study 1 nouns missing. So the retest analyses cover the `r dplyr::n_distinct(english_sample2$word)` nouns present in both samples (each participant rated a randomized 20-noun subset of the list, plus practice and check items). The absent nouns did not differ detectably from the covered nouns in the initial shape ratings (`r m_miss("shape_prop", TRUE)` vs. `r m_miss("shape_prop", FALSE)`, Welch `r fmt_p(tt_miss_shape$p.value)`); wherever later analyses average the two samples, these nouns carry their initial-sample value alone (Study 4).

#### Procedure

The experiment started with familiarization trials of what a category-organizing or characterizing feature means. However, this time the instructions were improved with more examples, adding picture depictions, training questions with feedback and clarifications. Examples involved answers that correspond to all 4 answer options "shape, material, color, none of these" so not to bias subjects into a specific answer, using examples like "Pottery, red traffic light, happiness, and ball". The rest of the study was similar to Study 1. Browser-ready experiment files in the shared files 

### Results

The overall distribution of shape-based categorization responses did not significantly differ from the initial sample and shows a general group-level agreement. Mixed-effects modeling showed that ratings in the retest were slightly but significantly lower than in the initial sample (`r sprintf("$B$ = %s, %s", papaja::printnum(eng_cmp_B, digits = 2), fmt_p(eng_cmp_p))`), suggesting that more scaffolding and instructions led to more conservative shape ratings (Figure \@ref(fig:enggrplevel)).

Paired comparisons of the shape ratings at the word level showed a raw correlation of $r$ = `r round(overall_reliability$estimate, 2)` and a Spearman--Brown predicted reliability of `r round(predicted_reliability, 2)` for the two-sample average (Figure \@ref(fig:relwordlvl)).
Some household items received more differentiated shape-based ratings than we expected: although one might think all "knives" share a shape, raters may have considered the different types of knives (e.g., butter knife, pocket knife, chef's knife) when rating the organizing feature.

## Discussion

In two samples, we found that the lexical statistics were homogeneous across the 16 languages we sampled. Two interpretations of this cross-linguistic null are available, and the design of Study 1 cannot distinguish them. On a strong reading, the lexical statistics of early lexicons everywhere are dominated by solid, count nouns with a less degree of shape coherence, and the cross-linguistic variation in the child shape bias is therefore not a downstream consequence of cross-linguistic variation in lexical statistics. On a weaker reading, the Study 1 design is by construction insensitive to such variation, because rater language is held constant and any conceptual differences between language communities are projected onto a single English judgment. Study 2 is designed to distinguish them by replicating the rating task with Korean-speaking adults rating Korean CDI items.
Given the reasonable reliability of the organizing-feature measure across the two samples and the strong word-level correlation, we use the mean shape ratings (averaged across the initial and retest samples) in subsequent analyses, and conduct sensitivity analyses that exclude words with the largest between-study differences. Recomputing the conditional analysis on this averaged measure leaves it essentially unchanged: among the `r n_cond80` nouns meeting the 80% solidity and count criteria, mean shape is `r m_cond80_avg` and `r pct_cond80_avg`% meet the 80% shape criterion.

# Study 2: Rating lexical statistics in Korean

While the shape-based categorization results from English speakers provided a useful benchmark, we next assess whether similar patterns would emerge in speakers of typologically different languages. Korean, with its distinct morphological and syntactic structures, offered an ideal test case to examine the cross-linguistic generalizability of shape-based categorization tendencies observed in English speakers. Korean language was also chosen because previous research has shown that Korean-speaking children, as well as other East Asian languages, exhibit a lower level of shape bias in early noun learning. If the distributional account of the shape bias is correct, we would expect to find a lower proportion of nouns rated as organized by shape in Korean compared to English, along with weaker correlations between shape-based categorization and the other dimensions.

We collected two Korean samples: an in-country sample that followed the @samuelson1999 procedure, and an online sample matched to the single-forced-choice procedure of Study 1. The matched sample provides the primary comparison with the English ratings.

## The in-country sample

This first Korean sample was collected in South Korea through a collaborator at Chosun University. The procedure for the category-organizing block followed the @samuelson1999 design in allowing multiple feature selections and in presenting words grouped by semantic category, and so differed from Study 1 in more than the raters' language. These procedural differences matter for interpreting the absolute level of the shape ratings, and we return to them in Study 3.

# English raters' judgments (Study 1A) of the Korean CDI unilemma set, for the
# cross-rater comparison reported in this and the following study.
english_sample1_koreanlist <- english_sample1 %>% filter (language == "Korean")

  mutate(

#### Participants

A total of `r length(unique(korean_demo_sample2$participant_id))` Korean-speaking adults were recruited through a local platform at Chosun University in South Korea (mean age = `r round(tidy$mean_age,2)`, SD = `r round(tidy$sd_age,2)`).

#### Material

The same subset of words from the Korean CDI reports on the Wordbank repository as used in Study 1. But instead of using the unilemmas, we used the Korean nouns.

#### Procedure

The task was translated to Korean by a native speaker, and validated by other native speakers. The presentation followed @samuelson1999 which differed from Study 1 in three respects. First, participants rated the full word list within each block, and the blocks appeared in a fixed order (solidity, then countable/uncountable, then category-organizing feature) rather than in a randomized order with word subsets. The countability here is a semantic status not a syntactic one. Second, in the category-organizing block, participants were allowed to select multiple organizing features (shape, color, material, not applicable) per item. Third, items in that block were presented grouped by semantic category (e.g., fruits, vehicles, furniture) rather than randomly intermixed.

##### Coding of the category-organizing feature for cross-study comparison.

To compare the multiple-selection responses in this sample to the single-selection responses in Study 1, we adopted a conservative coding: an item is treated as having "shape" as its organizing feature only when shape was the sole feature selected on that trial. Responses where shape was selected alongside another feature (e.g., "shape and material") were retained in the dataset but classified as "multiple". Below we report the strict-coding results in the main text and a sensitivity analysis using the broader coding ("shape selected, alone or alongside another feature") to quantify how much the coding decision matters.

### Results and discussion

```{r }
summary_kor_2 <- korean_sample2 %>% group_by(matching_response, block) %>% summarize(mean_prop = mean(proportion), sd_prop= sd(proportion))

korean_sample2 %>% select(block, matching_response, cleaned_response) %>% distinct()
```

```{r kor2-sensitivity}
# Sensitivity analysis for Study 2A: strict ("shape only") vs. broad
# ("shape selected alone or alongside another feature") coding of the
# category-organizing feature. The strict coding is what is used in the
# main shape proportion; the broad coding adds the multiple-selection
# trials whose response string includes "form" (the Korean response label
# that maps to "shape").

shape_strict_kor2 <- korean_sample2 %>%
  filter(block == "category_organization", matching_response == "shape") %>%
  distinct(Word, proportion) %>%
  rename(prop_strict = proportion)

shape_broad_kor2 <- korean_sample2 %>%
  filter(block == "category_organization") %>%
  filter(matching_response == "shape" |
           (matching_response == "multiple" &
              stringr::str_detect(cleaned_response, "form"))) %>%
  group_by(Word) %>%
  summarise(prop_broad = sum(proportion), .groups = "drop")

all_kor2_words <- korean_sample2 %>%
  filter(block == "category_organization") %>%
  distinct(Word)

shape_kor2_compare <- all_kor2_words %>%
  left_join(shape_strict_kor2, by = "Word") %>%
  left_join(shape_broad_kor2, by = "Word") %>%
  mutate(
    prop_strict = replace_na(prop_strict, 0),
    prop_broad  = replace_na(prop_broad, 0)
  )

m_shape_2a <- mean(shape_kor2_compare$prop_strict, na.rm = TRUE)
sd_shape_2a <- sd(shape_kor2_compare$prop_strict, na.rm = TRUE)

# Counts of trials, weighting per-word proportions by per-word total count
n_trials_total <- korean_sample2 %>%
  filter(block == "category_organization") %>%
  distinct(Word, totcount) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(totcount, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(n)

n_shape_only <- korean_sample2 %>%
  filter(block == "category_organization", matching_response == "shape") %>%
  summarise(n = sum(proportion * totcount, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(n) %>% round()

n_shape_multi <- korean_sample2 %>%
  filter(block == "category_organization",
         matching_response == "multiple",
         stringr::str_detect(cleaned_response, "form")) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(proportion * totcount, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(n) %>% round()

mean_shape_strict <- mean(shape_kor2_compare$prop_strict, na.rm = TRUE)
sd_shape_strict   <- sd(shape_kor2_compare$prop_strict,   na.rm = TRUE)
mean_shape_broad  <- mean(shape_kor2_compare$prop_broad,  na.rm = TRUE)
sd_shape_broad    <- sd(shape_kor2_compare$prop_broad,    na.rm = TRUE)

# Single source of record for the Study 2A coding-sensitivity numbers: the
# supplement table reads this CSV, so main text and supplement cannot diverge.
write_csv(
  tibble::tibble(
    statistic = c("organizing_trials_total", "shape_only_trials",
                  "shape_plus_other_trials", "mean_strict", "sd_strict",
                  "mean_broad", "sd_broad", "n_items"),
    value = c(n_trials_total, n_shape_only, n_shape_multi,
              mean_shape_strict, sd_shape_strict,
              mean_shape_broad, sd_shape_broad, nrow(shape_kor2_compare))
  ),
  here("data/predictors", "study2a_shape_coding_sensitivity.csv"))
```

We collected a total of `r prettyNum(n_ratings_of(korean_sample2, "uni_lemma"), big.mark = ",")` ratings across `r length(unique(korean_demo_sample2$participant_id))` participants for `r length(unique(korean_sample2$uni_lemma))` nouns in three blocks (solidity, countability, and category-organizing feature). Nouns received an average of `r korean_sample2 %>% dplyr::distinct(uni_lemma, block, totcount) %>% dplyr::summarise(a = mean(totcount, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% dplyr::pull(a) %>% round(2)` ratings per noun per block.

Across participants, nouns were predominantly rated as solid (M = `r round(summary_kor_2$mean_prop[summary_kor_2$matching_response == "solid"],2)`, SD = `r round(summary_kor_2$sd_prop[summary_kor_2$matching_response == "solid"],2)`) and countable (M = `r round(summary_kor_2$mean_prop[summary_kor_2$matching_response == "count"],2)`, SD = `r round(summary_kor_2$sd_prop[summary_kor_2$matching_response == "count"],2)` ), consistent with the English samples. The shape ratings were not. Under the strict coding, the mean shape proportion was M = `r round(m_shape_2a, 2)` (SD = `r round(sd_shape_2a, 2)`), higher than the English estimates for the same Korean-CDI items as rated by English speakers (M = `r m_ek("shape")`, SD = `r sd_ek("shape")`).

**Sensitivity analysis: strict vs. broad coding of shape** Of the `r prettyNum(n_trials_total, big.mark = ",")` category-organizing-feature trials in this sample, approximately `r prettyNum(n_shape_only, big.mark = ",")` were "shape only" responses and `r prettyNum(n_shape_multi, big.mark = ",")` selected shape alongside at least one other feature. Under the strict coding used in the main analysis, the mean shape proportion was `r round(mean_shape_strict, 2)` (SD = `r round(sd_shape_strict, 2)`); under the broader coding the mean shape proportion rose to `r round(mean_shape_broad, 2)` (SD = `r round(sd_shape_broad, 2)`). Under either coding, however, the Korean ratings are higher than the English ratings of the same items.
Korean raters might be perceiving these noun categories as more shape-organized than English raters do. It could also be procedural: multiple selection, semantic grouping, and the fixed presentation each differ from Study 1. The matched forced-choice sample below addresses the first by repeating the rating task with Korean speakers under the exact single-forced-choice procedure of Study 1, and Study 3 addresses the second by manipulating the procedural factors directly in English samples.

## The matched forced-choice sample

We collected a second Korean sample with the procedure held identical to Study 1: the same single forced choice and the same randomized presentation used in Study 1. If the higher shape ratings in the in-country sample were produced entirely by its procedure, this sample should look like the English samples. If Korean raters judge these categories as more shape-organized regardless of procedure, the ratings should remain elevated.

### Methods

#### Procedure

The procedure was the same as in the Study 1 retest, translated to Korean by a native speaker, and validated by other native speakers who were blinded to the purpose of the study and its theoretical background. Unlike the in-country sample, participants made a single forced choice on every trial, rated a randomized subset of 20 nouns per block, and no semantic-category information was provided.

### Results and discussion

```{r kor-eng-contrast}
# Inferential contrast for the Korean (2B) vs. English (1A, Korean-CDI list)
# shape comparison: paired item-level difference with a bootstrap CI and
# Cohen's d_z, plus a binomial GLMM on per-item counts of shape choices with
# a random intercept for item. The archived data for these two samples are
# aggregated within items, so participant-level random effects are not
# estimable here; trial-level models appear in Study 3.
s_ek_uni <- shape_prop_per_item(english_sample1_koreanlist, "uni_lemma") %>%
  rename(shape_eng = shape_prop)
ek_paired <- s_ek_uni %>%
  inner_join(s2b_shape %>% rename(shape_kor = shape_prop), by = "uni_lemma") %>%
  mutate(diff = shape_kor - shape_eng)
n_ek_paired <- nrow(ek_paired)
m_ek_diff   <- mean(ek_paired$diff)
set.seed(42)
ek_boots   <- replicate(5000, mean(sample(ek_paired$diff, replace = TRUE)))
ek_ci_low  <- quantile(ek_boots, 0.025)
ek_ci_high <- quantile(ek_boots, 0.975)
ek_dz      <- m_ek_diff / sd(ek_paired$diff)

item_shape_counts <- function(df, item_col, rater_label) {
  block_df <- df %>% filter(block == "category_organization")
  tot <- block_df %>% distinct(.data[[item_col]], totcount) %>%
    group_by(.data[[item_col]]) %>%
    summarise(n = max(totcount), .groups = "drop")
  k <- block_df %>% filter(matching_response == "shape") %>%
    distinct(.data[[item_col]], count) %>%
    group_by(.data[[item_col]]) %>%
    summarise(k = sum(count), .groups = "drop")
  tot %>% left_join(k, by = item_col) %>%
    mutate(k = replace_na(k, 0), rater = rater_label) %>%
    rename(uni_lemma = all_of(item_col))
}
ek_glmm_df <- bind_rows(
  item_shape_counts(english_sample1_koreanlist, "uni_lemma", "English"),
  item_shape_counts(korean_sample1, "uni_lemma", "Korean")
) %>%
  filter(uni_lemma %in% ek_paired$uni_lemma) %>%
  mutate(rater = factor(rater, levels = c("English", "Korean")))
ek_glmm <- lme4::glmer(cbind(k, n - k) ~ rater + (1 | uni_lemma),
                       data = ek_glmm_df, family = binomial)
ek_glmm_coefs <- summary(ek_glmm)$coefficients
ek_or    <- exp(lme4::fixef(ek_glmm)["raterKorean"])
ek_or_ci <- exp(confint(ek_glmm, parm = "raterKorean", method = "Wald"))
ek_glmm_p <- ek_glmm_coefs["raterKorean", "Pr(>|z|)"]

kor1_item_counts <- korean_sample1 %>%
  filter(block == "category_organization") %>%
  distinct(uni_lemma, totcount)
med_ratings_2b <- median(kor1_item_counts$totcount)
iqr_lo_2b <- quantile(kor1_item_counts$totcount, 0.25)
iqr_hi_2b <- quantile(kor1_item_counts$totcount, 0.75)

# One-to-one mapping check for the translation-granularity confound,
# precomputed by analysis/aoa-power-bayes.R (re-run that script before
# knitting after any rating-data update).

# Study labels follow the manuscript numbering: 2A = in-country (Chosun)
# sample (korean_sample2 data), 2B = online forced-choice sample
# (korean_sample1 data). 2A is the reference level, so the study2B
# coefficient estimates the change from the in-country to the online sample.
study2a_shape_tbl <- shape_prop_per_item(korean_sample2, "uni_lemma") %>%
  transmute(uni_lemma, shape_rating = shape_prop, study = "2A")

  transmute(uni_lemma, shape_rating = shape_prop, study = "2B")

combined_kor_shape <- bind_rows(study2a_shape_tbl, study2b_shape_tbl) %>%
  filter(!is.na(shape_rating)) %>%
  mutate(
    shape_rating = as.numeric(shape_rating),
    study = factor(study, levels = c("2A", "2B"))
  ) %>%
  distinct()

kor_comparison_model <- lmer(shape_rating ~ study + (1 | uni_lemma),
                             data = combined_kor_shape)

long_data <- all_data_long %>%
  mutate(
    language = case_when(
      sample %in% c("eng1", "eng2") ~ "English",
      sample %in% c("kor1", "kor2") ~ "Korean"
    )
  )

lang_means <- long_data %>%
  group_by(uni_lemma, response_norm, block, language) %>%
  summarise(proportion = mean(proportion), .groups = "drop")

lang_means_wide <- lang_means %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = language, values_from = proportion)

# Pooled over solidity, count, and shape blocks (same paired rows as below).
r_engkor_pooled <- cor(lang_means_wide$English, lang_means_wide$Korean, use = "pairwise")
# Item-level: shape-organization in the category-organizing block only (transparency).
lang_means_shape_org <- lang_means_wide %>%
  filter(response_norm == "shape", block == "category_organization")
n_shape_paired_ek  <- sum(complete.cases(lang_means_shape_org$English, lang_means_shape_org$Korean))
r_engkor_shape_bco <- cor(lang_means_shape_org$English, lang_means_shape_org$Korean,
                          use = "pairwise.complete.obs") %>% as.numeric()

# Per-block cross-rater correlations, reported separately because pooling
# blocks lets the high-agreement dimensions (solidity, count) carry the
# pooled correlation.
r_engkor_block <- function(rn, bl) {
  d <- lang_means_wide %>% filter(response_norm == rn, block == bl)
  cor(d$English, d$Korean, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
}
r_engkor_solid <- r_engkor_block("solid", "solidity")
r_engkor_count <- r_engkor_block("count", "count_mass")
```

We collected `r prettyNum(n_ratings_of(korean_sample1, "uni_lemma"), big.mark = ",")` ratings across `r length(unique(korean_demo_sample1$participant_id))` participants for `r length(unique(korean_sample1$uni_lemma))` nouns in three blocks (solidity, count-mass syntax, and category-organizing feature), after dropping practice, attention-check, and no recorded response trials. Nouns received an average of `r korean_sample1 %>% dplyr::distinct(uni_lemma, block, totcount) %>% dplyr::summarise(a = mean(totcount, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% dplyr::pull(a) %>% round(2)` ratings per block.

Overall, nouns were predominantly rated as solid (M = `r m_k1("solid")`, SD = `r sd_k1("solid")`) and countable (M = `r m_k1("countable")`, SD = `r sd_k1("countable")`), but were less reliably judged as being organized by shape (M = `r m_k1("shape")`, SD = `r sd_k1("shape")`). Korean adult ratings were therefore comparable to English raters on solidity and countability, but higher in shape.
Pearson correlation analysis revealed a moderate positive correlation between solidity and count syntax ($r$ = `r r_k1("countable", "solid")`, `r fmt_p(p_k1("countable", "solid"))`), a weak positive correlation between count syntax and shape-based categorization ($r$ = `r r_k1("countable", "shape")`, `r fmt_p(p_k1("countable", "shape"))`), and between solidity and shape-based categorization ($r$ = `r r_k1("solid", "shape")`, `r fmt_p(p_k1("solid", "shape"))`). 
The Euler diagram in Figure \@ref(fig:vennkorean1) shows categories of nouns as solid, count noun, and shape-characterized using the cutoff of 80%. A larger number of nouns were categorized as shape-based in Korean compared to English.
A binomial mixed-effects model of the per-item counts of shape choices, with rater language as a fixed effect and a random intercept for item, showed the same contrast (odds ratio = `r papaja::printnum(ek_or, digits = 2)`, 95% CI [`r papaja::printnum(ek_or_ci[1], digits = 2)`, `r papaja::printnum(ek_or_ci[2], digits = 2)`], `r fmt_p(ek_glmm_p)`). `r ek_121_n` of the `r n_ek_paired` shared items map a single Korean CDI item to a single unilemma in both datasets, so the contrast is not an artifact of translation granularity and restricting the comparison to that subset left the difference unchanged (`r papaja::printnum(ek_121_diff, digits = 2)`, bootstrap 95% CI [`r papaja::printnum(ek_121_lo, digits = 2)`, `r papaja::printnum(ek_121_hi, digits = 2)`]).

This matched procedure produced lower shape ratings than the in-country sample: a mixed-effects model comparing the two showed that shape ratings in the matched sample were lower than in the in-country sample (`r sprintf("$B$ = %s, %s", papaja::printnum(kor_cmp_B, digits = 2), fmt_p(kor_cmp_p))`). This pattern is consistent with part of the in-country level being produced by its procedure (multiple selection, semantic grouping, fixed presentation) and part reflecting a rater-language difference that survives full procedure matching. Figure \@ref(fig:4-smpls) shows the word-level distributions for all four norming samples.

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\centering
\captionsetup{font=tiny,skip=1pt,labelfont=tiny,textfont=tiny}
\includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{data/figures/4_smpls.png}
\caption{Word-level shape-organization proportions across the four rater samples (strict coding for the in-country Korean sample). Boxplots are the median and interquartile range; each violin includes only the items rated in that sample.}
\label{fig:4-smpls}
\end{figure}

Item-level shape proportions show a correlation of $r$ = `r round(predicted_reliability_within_kor,2)` with Spearman–Brown correction. The two samples largely agree on which nouns are more shape-organized than others (rank-order consistency), even though their absolute levels differ in the direction just described. Item-level means across English and procedure-matched Korean correlated at $r$ = `r round(r_engkor_shape_bco, 2)` for shape ($N$ = `r n_shape_paired_ek` items with complete pairs); $r$ = `r round(r_engkor_solid, 2)` for solidity and $r$ = `r round(r_engkor_count, 2)` for countability. 

```{r commitment-check, include=FALSE}
# Response-style check for the Korean-English contrast: residual-option use,
# full four-way response shares, shape as a share of committed
# (shape/color/material) responses, and a committed-only refit of the
# binomial mixed-effects model above.
eng_none_kl <- english_sample1_koreanlist %>%
  dplyr::filter(block == "category_organization") %>%
  dplyr::distinct(uni_lemma, response, count) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(s = sum(count[response == "none of these"]) / sum(count)) %>%
  dplyr::pull(s)
kor_none_2b <- korean_sample1 %>%
  dplyr::filter(block == "category_organization") %>%
  dplyr::distinct(uni_lemma, eng_response, count) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(s = sum(count[eng_response == "not applicable"]) / sum(count)) %>%
  dplyr::pull(s)
eng_kl_share <- english_sample1_koreanlist %>%
  dplyr::filter(block == "category_organization") %>%
  dplyr::distinct(uni_lemma, response, count) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(response) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(k = sum(count), .groups = "drop") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(s = k / sum(k))
kor_2b_share <- korean_sample1 %>%
  dplyr::filter(block == "category_organization") %>%
  dplyr::distinct(uni_lemma, eng_response, count) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(eng_response) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(k = sum(count), .groups = "drop") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(s = k / sum(k))
esh_kl <- function(r) sprintf("%.0f", 100 * eng_kl_share$s[eng_kl_share$response == r])
ksh_2b <- function(r) sprintf("%.0f", 100 * kor_2b_share$s[kor_2b_share$eng_response == r])
comm_kor <- korean_sample1 %>%
  dplyr::filter(block == "category_organization",
                eng_response %in% c("form", "color", "substance")) %>%
  dplyr::distinct(uni_lemma, eng_response, count) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(item = tolower(uni_lemma)) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(kor = sum(count[eng_response == "form"]) / sum(count),
                   .groups = "drop")
comm_eng <- english_sample1_koreanlist %>%
  dplyr::filter(block == "category_organization",
                matching_response %in% c("shape", "color", "material")) %>%
  dplyr::distinct(uni_lemma, matching_response, count) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(item = tolower(uni_lemma)) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(eng = sum(count[matching_response == "shape"]) / sum(count),
                   .groups = "drop")
comm_paired <- dplyr::inner_join(comm_eng, comm_kor, by = "item") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(diff = kor - eng)
set.seed(11)
comm_boot   <- replicate(5000, mean(sample(comm_paired$diff, replace = TRUE)))
comm_diff_m <- sprintf("%.3f", mean(comm_paired$diff))
comm_ci     <- sprintf("%.3f", quantile(comm_boot, c(.025, .975)))
comm_counts <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  english_sample1_koreanlist %>%
    dplyr::filter(block == "category_organization",
                  matching_response %in% c("shape", "color", "material")) %>%
    dplyr::distinct(uni_lemma, matching_response, count) %>%
    dplyr::group_by(item = tolower(uni_lemma)) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(k = sum(count[matching_response == "shape"]),
                     n = sum(count), .groups = "drop") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(rater = "English"),
  korean_sample1 %>%
    dplyr::filter(block == "category_organization",
                  eng_response %in% c("form", "color", "substance")) %>%
    dplyr::distinct(uni_lemma, eng_response, count) %>%
    dplyr::group_by(item = tolower(uni_lemma)) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(k = sum(count[eng_response == "form"]),
                     n = sum(count), .groups = "drop") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(rater = "Korean")
) %>%
  dplyr::filter(item %in% comm_paired$item, n > 0)
comm_glmm   <- lme4::glmer(cbind(k, n - k) ~ rater + (1 | item),
                           family = binomial, data = comm_counts)
comm_or     <- exp(lme4::fixef(comm_glmm)["raterKorean"])
comm_or_ci  <- exp(confint(comm_glmm, parm = "raterKorean", method = "Wald"))
comm_glmm_p <- summary(comm_glmm)$coefficients["raterKorean", "Pr(>|z|)"]
```

Korean raters in this sample chose the not-applicable option far less often than English raters in Study 1 did none of these (`r round(100 * kor_none_2b)`% vs. `r round(100 * eng_none_kl)`% of organizing-feature trials), and the difference was distributed over both shape (`r ksh_2b("form")`% vs. `r esh_kl("shape")`% of responses) and material (`r ksh_2b("substance")`% vs. `r esh_kl("material")`%), with rare color in both groups (`r ksh_2b("color")`% and `r esh_kl("color")`%). The difference therefore also reflects a greater Korean willingness to commit to a single organizing feature, so the two rater groups differ in how much feature-based structure they attribute to the same items, not merely in response style.

# Study 3: Procedural determinants of shape ratings

Study 2 leaves a methodological question open: raters could select multiple organizing features, and words were presented grouped by semantic category, which means the comparisons may be partially a product of procedural choices. Study 3 therefore asks which procedural factors move shape ratings, when language is held constant.

## The multiple-selection format with random order

```{r eng3-multiselect}
# English multiple-selection samples on the same organizing-feature block as
# Studies 1A/1B, recovering the response format of Samuelson & Smith (1999):
# (i) random word order (format change only), and (ii) words grouped by
# semantic category (format + grouping, as in Study 2A).
parse_q0 <- function(x) {
  out <- tryCatch(jsonlite::fromJSON(x)$Q0, error = function(e) NA_character_)
  if (is.null(out)) NA_character_ else as.character(out)
}
load_ms_sample <- function(file) {
  raw <- read_csv(here("data/third-sample-english-multi-select", file),
                  show_col_types = FALSE)
  ms <- raw %>%
    filter(trial_type == "survey-multi-select",
           stringr::str_detect(block, "^category_organization"),
           !is.na(response), !is.na(theword)) %>%
    mutate(selected = purrr::map(response, parse_q0))
  # Attention check: the probe word "lavender" must be answered "none of these".
  att <- ms %>%
    filter(theword == "lavender") %>%
    mutate(pass = purrr::map_lgl(selected, ~ length(.x) == 1 && .x == "none of these")) %>%
    group_by(subject) %>%
    summarise(att_pass = all(pass), .groups = "drop")
  ms %>%
    filter(theword != "lavender") %>%
    left_join(att, by = "subject") %>%
    filter(att_pass) %>%
    mutate(
      n_sel      = purrr::map_int(selected, length),
      has_shape  = purrr::map_lgl(selected, ~ "shape" %in% .x),
      excl_shape = purrr::map_lgl(selected, ~ length(.x) == 1 && .x == "shape")
    )
}

eng3 <- load_ms_sample("samah.category_ms.csv")

n3_subj    <- dplyr::n_distinct(eng3$subject)
mean_sel3  <- round(mean(eng3$n_sel), 2)
pct_multi3 <- sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(eng3$n_sel > 1))

eng3_item <- eng3 %>%
  group_by(theword) %>%
  summarise(n_raters    = n(),
            shape_broad = mean(has_shape),
            shape_excl  = mean(excl_shape),
            .groups = "drop")
med_raters3 <- median(eng3_item$n_raters)

# Single-forced-choice shape per noun (all words in block; 0 if no shape vote).
single_choice_shape <- bind_rows(
  shape_prop_per_item(english_sample1, "word") %>%
    transmute(theword = word, shape_single = shape_prop),
  shape_prop_per_item(english_sample2, "word") %>%
    transmute(theword = word, shape_single = shape_prop)
) %>%
  group_by(theword) %>%
  summarise(shape_single = mean(shape_single, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

eng3_matched <- eng3_item %>% inner_join(single_choice_shape, by = "theword")
n3_matched  <- nrow(eng3_matched)
m_single3_r <- mean(eng3_matched$shape_single)
m_broad3_r  <- mean(eng3_matched$shape_broad)
m_excl3_r   <- mean(eng3_matched$shape_excl)
m_single3   <- round(m_single3_r, 2)
m_broad3    <- round(m_broad3_r, 2)
m_excl3     <- round(m_excl3_r, 2)
```

We first collected an English speaking sample (`r n3_subj` adults on Prolific who passed the attention check) that rated the same nouns on the organizing-feature block but recovered the original multiple-selection format, in which raters could endorse any combination of shape, color, material, or none of these. Word order remained fully randomized, so this sample changed only the response format. Raters seldom selected more than one feature on `r pct_multi3`% of trials (mean `r mean_sel3` selections per trial). On the `r n3_matched` nouns shared with Study 1, a broad coded shape count gave a mean shape proportion of `r m_broad3`, barely above the single-forced-choice estimate for the same nouns (`r m_single3`; the Study 1 two-sample average); coding shape only when it was selected alone gave `r m_excl3`.

## Adding semantic grouping

```{r eng-blocked-pilot}
# Same multiple-selection task, but words grouped by semantic category as in
# Study 2A and Samuelson & Smith (1999).
eng_blk <- load_ms_sample("samah.category_ms_blockeds.csv")

n_blk_subj        <- dplyr::n_distinct(eng_blk$subject)
mean_sel_blk      <- round(mean(eng_blk$n_sel), 2)
pct_multi_blkpilot <- sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(eng_blk$n_sel > 1))

eng_blk_item <- eng_blk %>%
  group_by(theword) %>%
  summarise(n_raters    = n(),
            shape_broad = mean(has_shape),
            shape_excl  = mean(excl_shape),
            .groups = "drop")
m_broad_blkpilot <- round(mean(eng_blk_item$shape_broad), 2)
m_excl_blkpilot  <- round(mean(eng_blk_item$shape_excl), 2)
med_raters_blk   <- median(eng_blk_item$n_raters)
```

A second English sample (`r n_blk_subj` adults passing the same attention check) completed the same multiple-selection task with the words grouped by semantic category: all members of one category (e.g., fruits) appeared in sequence before the next category began, and participants were told which category they were about to rate. Grouping changed behavior substantially. Raters selected more than one feature on `r pct_multi_blkpilot`% of trials (mean `r mean_sel_blk` selections per trial, against `r pct_multi3`% and `r mean_sel3` with random order), and broad-coded shape rose to `r m_broad_blkpilot` while strict-coded shape stayed at `r m_excl_blkpilot` (a median of `r med_raters_blk` raters per noun, so we treat these as sample-level descriptives). Because these two samples were collected separately rather than assigned at random, we treated this contrast as preliminary and ran a randomized experiment crossing the two factors.

## A randomized 2 $\times$ 2 experiment

```{r format-blocking-2x2-load, include=FALSE}
# Precomputed by analysis/format-blocking-2x2-participant-quality.R,

n_excl_fast    <- sum(fb_quality$flag_fast)
n_excl_id      <- sum(fb_quality$flag_explicit_id)

# Accessors for GLMM coefficients (trial-level logistic mixed models fit in
# analysis/format-blocking-2x2.R; random intercepts for subject and word).
fb_b <- function(model_name, term_name) {
  fb_models %>% dplyr::filter(model == model_name, term == term_name) %>%
    dplyr::pull(estimate) %>% dplyr::first()
}
fb_p <- function(model_name, term_name) {
  fb_models %>% dplyr::filter(model == model_name, term == term_name) %>%
    dplyr::pull(p.value) %>% dplyr::first()
}
fb_coef_txt <- function(model_name, term_name) {
  sprintf("$b$ = %s, %s",
          papaja::printnum(fb_b(model_name, term_name), digits = 2),
          fmt_p(fb_p(model_name, term_name)))
}

fb_table_df <- fb_cells %>%
  left_join(fb_design %>% select(format, blocking, n_subj), by = c("format", "blocking")) %>%

    Condition = paste(format, dplyr::recode(blocking, Blocked = "Grouped"),

m_ms_rand_strict <- fb_cells$strict_M[fb_cells$format == "Multi-select" &

fb_rate <- function(col, fmt, blk) {

}
```

### Methods

We ran a $2 \times 2$ experiment with random assignment of response format (single forced choice FC vs. multiple selection MS) crossed with item order (random vs. grouped by semantic category). Of `r n_2x2_screened` English speaking participants, `r n_2x2_total` trials retained after excluding participants who failed the attention check ($n$ = `r n_excl_att`), responded implausibly fast (median response time under 1.5 s, or half or more of trials under 1 s; $n$ = `r n_excl_fast`), or matched known invalid session identifiers ($n$ = `r n_excl_id`; flags overlap); retained cell sizes appear in Table \@ref(tab:format-blocking-2x2-table).

### Results

On the broad outcome, MS (`r fb_coef_txt("broad", "formatMulti-select")`) and semantic grouping (`r fb_coef_txt("broad", "blockingBlocked")`) each raised shape, with no interaction (`r fb_coef_txt("broad", "formatMulti-select:blockingBlocked")`). On the strict outcome, grouping raised shape under FC (`r fb_coef_txt("fc_blocking", "blockingBlocked")`; cell means `r sprintf("%.2f", m_fc_rand_2x2)` random vs. `r sprintf("%.2f", m_fc_blk_2x2)` grouped) and lowered it under MS (`r fb_coef_txt("ms_strict", "blockingBlocked")`; cell means `r sprintf("%.2f", m_ms_rand_strict)` random vs. `r sprintf("%.2f", m_ms_blk_strict)` grouped), producing a format by grouping interaction (`r fb_coef_txt("strict", "formatMulti-select:blockingBlocked")`). 
Grouping nearly doubled the rate of co-selection generally (`r sprintf("%.0f", pct_multi_rand)`% of random-order trials vs. `r sprintf("%.0f", pct_multi_blk)`% grouped; `r fb_coef_txt("multi_rate", "blockingBlocked")`), also raising color (selection rate `r sprintf("%.2f", fb_rate("rate_color", "Multi-select", "Random"))` random vs. `r sprintf("%.2f", fb_rate("rate_color", "Multi-select", "Blocked"))` grouped) and material (`r sprintf("%.2f", fb_rate("rate_material", "Multi-select", "Random"))` vs. `r sprintf("%.2f", fb_rate("rate_material", "Multi-select", "Blocked"))`) alongside shape while the rate of "none of these" fell (`r sprintf("%.2f", fb_rate("rate_none", "Multi-select", "Random"))` vs. `r sprintf("%.2f", fb_rate("rate_none", "Multi-select", "Blocked"))`). Figure \@ref(fig:allsamplesfig) shows that shape's broad advantage in MS is inherited from its strict advantage not when it is always selected with other dimensions.

On `r equiv_fc05$n_words` nouns rated in both the FC with random order condition and Study 1, the paired difference was `r sprintf("%.3f", equiv_fc05$mean_diff)` (95% CI [`r sprintf("%.3f", equiv_fc05$ci_low)`, `r sprintf("%.3f", equiv_fc05$ci_high)`], `r fmt_p(equiv_fc05$p_paired)`), with mean shape proportion of `r sprintf("%.2f", m_fc_rand_2x2)`. MS with random order depended on coding: strict shape (`r sprintf("%.2f", m_ms_rand_strict)`) was statistically equivalent to Study 1 within a $\pm 0.05$ margin, i.e., five percentage points (TOST, larger one-sided `r fmt_p(max(equiv_ms_strict$tost_p_low, equiv_ms_strict$tost_p_high))`), whereas broad shape rose to `r sprintf("%.2f", m_ms_rand_broad)`. 

```{r samples-summary-table, include=FALSE}
sample_row <- function(label, df, n_part, group_label, item_col = "uni_lemma") {
  # M/SD over per-item shape proportions; Ratings and Items use the same
  # definitions reused throughout the text (n_ratings_of and distinct items).
  sp <- shape_prop_per_item(df, item_col)
  tibble::tibble(
    Study   = label,
    Group   = group_label,
    N       = n_part,
    Items   = dplyr::n_distinct(df[[item_col]]),
    Ratings = prettyNum(round(n_ratings_of(df, item_col)), big.mark = ","),
    `M`     = sprintf("%.2f", mean(sp$shape_prop, na.rm = TRUE)),
    `SD`    = sprintf("%.2f", sd(sp$shape_prop, na.rm = TRUE))
  )
}
