### Discussion

Coding proportions strictly or broadly have the largest effect with the response format by itself (MS, FC) doing little. Semantic grouping moves both the FC measure and nearly doubles co-selection under MS resulting in an estimate of shape dominance that partly reflects procedure rather than the structure of the early lexicon. Aggregating every English MS grouped sample (the blocked pilot and the $2 \times 2$ grouped cell) yields the same mean broad shape (`r sprintf("%.2f", eng_agg_ms %>% filter(pool == "pooled_ms_blocked") %>% pull(mean_broad_shape))`) but still leaves only `r agg_ms_pct80_1a`% of Study 1 nouns above an 80% broad-shape cutoff, compared with the previous 48% at 85% agreement (Supplement S7).

Why does semantic grouping inflate the ratings? The selection behavior suggests a change in how raters construe the question rather than a change in what they believe about the categories. Raters endorsed more of everything, not more shape in particular. Presenting members of the same semantic category in sequence invites comparison among them, and comparison makes shared properties more salient [@gentner_markman_1997; @namy_gentner_2002]: when all the fruits arrive together, the rater's implicit comparison class shifts from nouns in general to the neighboring members of one category, and locally recurring properties become easy to endorse. One could defend grouped presentation as ecologically natural, since words might occur in semantically coherent contexts, but the rating task is a metalinguistic judgment by adults, not a word-learning episode, and grouping appears to change the judgment itself rather than bring it closer to a child's input; a word like "apple" is in any case encountered in diverse contexts, not only among other fruits "your shirt has an apple on it". 

Children's shape-bias tasks are FC extension tasks in which shape must win against a competing feature, so the adult statistic most comparable to the child data is the one produced under the same requirement to prioritize. We therefore use FC with random order (or its strict MS equivalent) as the standard for lexical-statistics claims throughout, and we use the strict coding for the in-country Korean sample wherever it enters later analyses. 

Finally, procedure does not close the cross-linguistic gap. The highest English estimate in any cell, broad-coded shape under grouped MS (`r sprintf("%.2f", m_ms_blk_broad)`), remains far below the in-country Korean sample under the matched broad coding (`r round(mean_shape_broad, 2)`) and does not exceed its strict coding (`r round(mean_shape_strict, 2)`); and the matched FC sample still shows Korean ratings above English ones, partly as the difference in commitment documented there.

# Study 4: Predicting age of acquisition

```{r aoa-data-load, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
aoa <- read_csv(here("data/predictors/aoa_predictor_data.csv")) %>%
  filter(measure == "produces") %>% select(-measure)

shape_s1_map <- shape_prop_per_item(english_sample1, "word") %>%
  left_join(english_sample1 %>% distinct(word, uni_lemma, language), by = "word") %>%
  select(uni_lemma, language, shape_s1 = shape_prop)
shape_s2_map <- shape_prop_per_item(english_sample2, "word") %>%
  left_join(english_sample2 %>% distinct(word, uni_lemma, language), by = "word") %>%
  select(uni_lemma, language, shape_s2 = shape_prop)

ratings_aoa <- read_csv(here("data/predictors", "ratings_aoa.csv")) %>%
  select(-any_of(c("mean_shape", "shape_s1", "shape_s2"))) %>%
  left_join(shape_s1_map, by = c("uni_lemma", "language")) %>%
  left_join(shape_s2_map, by = c("uni_lemma", "language"))
# Nouns with no retained Study 1B ratings keep their Study 1A value:
# zero-filling shape_s2 across samples would halve their mean shape
# (same cross-sample zero-fill bug fixed in the four-sample figure).
n_uni_s1_only <- ratings_aoa %>% filter(is.na(shape_s2)) %>%
  distinct(uni_lemma) %>% nrow()
ratings_aoa <- ratings_aoa %>%
  mutate(
    shape_s1   = replace_na(shape_s1, 0),
    mean_shape = if_else(is.na(shape_s2), shape_s1, (shape_s1 + shape_s2) / 2),
    shape_s2   = replace_na(shape_s2, 0)
  )
write_csv(ratings_aoa, here("data/predictors", "ratings_aoa.csv"))
```

Adult ratings show that shape-organized nouns are not overwhelmingly common among early nouns. In Study 4 we ask whether mean shape ratings still predict age of acquisition after controlling for frequency and related covariates: whether shape is a good cue for learning even when it is not a common one. 

## Methods

Our outcome variable is item-level age of acquisition (AoA) in months, derived from Wordbank parental-report data using the logistic-curve fitting procedure of @braginsky_2019. For each language and each CDI word, AoA is defined as the age (in months) at which the proportion of children reported to produce the word reaches 0.5 in cross-sectional production data. We use the publicly available AoA estimates released alongside Wordbank [@frank2021variability] and restrict to the production trajectory throughout. Using our shape-rating measures as a predictor of an independent and precomputed developmental measure data provides a form of external validation. This strategy follows a now-standard family of analyses in the early-noun literature [e.g., @braginsky_2019]. 

### Predictors

We model AoA as a function of five item-level predictors: Mean shape rating of the initial and retest study 1, count-noun and solid proportions from initial study 1, word frequency as the log relative frequency of the unilemma in the CHILDES corpus for that language, standardized within language, as distributed with Wordbank, and concreteness as adult concreteness norms from @brysbaert_etal_2014, which provides ratings for 40,000 English lemmas on a 1–5 scale. All continuous predictors are *z*-scored prior to fitting. AoA estimates were available for `r ratings_aoa %>% distinct(uni_lemma, language) %>% nrow()` item-by-language observations across `r length(unique(ratings_aoa$language))` languages (Wordbank production-AoA estimates were unavailable for Kiswahili and Spanish (Peruvian), so Study 4 covers 14 of the 16 Study 1 languages). Table \@ref(tab:samples-summary-table) summarizes sample sizes and mean shape-organization ratings for the four norming samples.

### Models


The first unilemma model is a linear mixed-effects regression of the form
$$
\small\begin{aligned}
\text{AoA}_i ={} & \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{logfreq}_i + \beta_2\,\text{concreteness}_i + \beta_3\,\text{solid}_i +\beta_4\,\text{count}_i + \beta_5\,\text{shape}_i + \beta_6\,\text{language}_i + u_{\text{category}[i]}+ v_{\text{unilemma}[i]}+ \epsilon_i \end{aligned}
$$
The shape, solidity, and count-noun predictors are English-rater judgments attached to a unilemma, so the cross-linguistic variation is therefore a variation in which unilemmas each language's early lexicon contains and in the AoA of those unilemmas. We additionally fit a sensitivity model restricted to artifact-leaning categories (excluding animals, body parts, clothing, and outside), since the development of word learning for animate and natural-kind nouns may follow a different trajectory.
We also fit a single-language English AoA model, and compare two Korean AoA models on the same matched item set to ask which rater group's lexical features better predict Korean AoA. The English-predictor model enters the average of study 1 ratings with Korean unilemma corpus frequency and concreteness. The Korean-predictor model enters the average of Study 2 ratings, with the same Korean corpus log frequency, but omits concreteness because those norms are English ratings rather than Korean-specific measures.

```{r aoa-models}
# Cross-linguistic mixed-effects model with crossed random effects for
# semantic category and unilemma (each concept recurs across languages).
full_fit   <- lmerTest::lmer(
  aoa ~ logfreq + concreteness + solid + mean_shape + count_noun + language +
        (1 | category) + (1 | uni_lemma),
  data = predictors_df_few)
full_model <- summary(full_fit)
full_coefs <- coef(full_model)

# Sensitivity model: artifacts only (drop animate / body / clothing / outside)
artifact_fit   <- lmerTest::lmer(
  aoa ~ logfreq + concreteness + solid + mean_shape + count_noun +
        (1 | language) + (1 | category) + (1 | uni_lemma),
  data = predictors_df_few %>%
    filter(!category %in% c("animals", "body parts", "clothing", "outside")))
artifact_coefs <- coef(summary(artifact_fit))

# Helper to format a single fixed-effect coefficient as "B = X.XX, p = .XXX".
fmt_coef <- function(coefs, term) {
  est <- coefs[term, "Estimate"]
  pv  <- coefs[term, "Pr(>|t|)"]
  sprintf("$B$ = %s, %s",
          papaja::printnum(est, digits = 2),
          fmt_p(pv))
}
```

```{r aoa-robustness}
# Robustness checks for the shape-AoA coefficient: (i) Wald CI and effect
# size in SD-of-AoA units; (ii) English (American) single-language fit,
# where no unilemma recurs; (iii) per-language random slope for shape;
# (iv) refits excluding the most widely shared unilemmas (top decile and
# top quartile of the number of language sets a unilemma appears in).
shape_wald_ci <- confint(full_fit, parm = "mean_shape", method = "Wald")
sd_aoa_s4     <- sd(predictors_df_few$aoa, na.rm = TRUE)
shape_std_b   <- full_coefs["mean_shape", "Estimate"] / sd_aoa_s4

engonly_df  <- predictors_df_few %>% filter(language == "English (American)")
engonly_fit <- lmerTest::lmer(
  aoa ~ logfreq + concreteness + solid + mean_shape + count_noun +
        (1 | category),
  data = engonly_df)
engonly_coefs <- coef(summary(engonly_fit))

slope_fit <- lmerTest::lmer(
  aoa ~ logfreq + concreteness + solid + mean_shape + count_noun +
        (1 | category) + (1 | uni_lemma) + (0 + mean_shape | language),
  data = predictors_df_few)
slope_coefs   <- coef(summary(slope_fit))
slope_sd_lang <- attr(lme4::VarCorr(slope_fit)$language, "stddev")[["mean_shape"]]

share_n <- predictors_df_few %>%
  distinct(uni_lemma, language) %>%
  count(uni_lemma, name = "n_lang")
refit_excl_shared <- function(q) {
  thr  <- quantile(share_n$n_lang, q)
  keep <- share_n %>% filter(n_lang <= thr) %>% pull(uni_lemma)
  dat  <- predictors_df_few %>% filter(uni_lemma %in% keep)
  fit  <- lmerTest::lmer(
    aoa ~ logfreq + concreteness + solid + mean_shape + count_noun + language +
          (1 | category) + (1 | uni_lemma),
    data = dat)
  list(coefs = coef(summary(fit)), n_uni = length(keep),
       n_rows = nrow(dat), thr = thr)
}
excl_decile   <- refit_excl_shared(0.90)
excl_quartile <- refit_excl_shared(0.75)
n_rows_s4     <- nrow(predictors_df_few)

# Reliability-matched refit: the Study 1A shape proportion in place of the
# two-sample average, so all three lexical predictors come from one sample
# with comparable rater counts.
s1only_fit <- lmerTest::lmer(
  aoa ~ logfreq + concreteness + solid + shape_s1 + count_noun + language +
        (1 | category) + (1 | uni_lemma),
  data = predictors_df_few)
s1only_coefs <- coef(summary(s1only_fit))
```

```{r aoa-lolo}
# Leave-one-language-out: refit the primary model 14 times, dropping one
# language's rows each time, to check that no single language carries the
# shape coefficient. Written to CSV for the supplement table.
lolo_langs <- sort(unique(predictors_df_few$language))
lolo_tbl <- purrr::map_dfr(lolo_langs, function(L) {
  d   <- predictors_df_few %>% filter(language != L)
  fit <- suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(lmerTest::lmer(
    aoa ~ logfreq + concreteness + solid + mean_shape + count_noun + language +
          (1 | category) + (1 | uni_lemma),
    data = d)))
  cf <- coef(summary(fit))["mean_shape", ]
  tibble::tibble(
    dropped_language = L,
    n_obs    = nrow(d),
    estimate = cf[["Estimate"]],
    se       = cf[["Std. Error"]],
    ci_low   = cf[["Estimate"]] - 1.96 * cf[["Std. Error"]],
    ci_high  = cf[["Estimate"]] + 1.96 * cf[["Std. Error"]],
    p        = cf[["Pr(>|t|)"]])
})
lolo_pooled <- tibble::tibble(
  dropped_language = "none (pooled model)",
  n_obs    = n_rows_s4,
  estimate = full_coefs[["mean_shape", "Estimate"]],
  se       = full_coefs[["mean_shape", "Std. Error"]],
  ci_low   = shape_wald_ci[[1]],
  ci_high  = shape_wald_ci[[2]],
  p        = full_coefs[["mean_shape", "Pr(>|t|)"]])
readr::write_csv(bind_rows(lolo_pooled, lolo_tbl),
                 here("data/predictors", "aoa_lolo_sensitivity.csv"))

lolo_n_neg   <- sum(lolo_tbl$estimate < 0)
lolo_n_sig   <- sum(lolo_tbl$p < .05)
lolo_min_est <- max(lolo_tbl$estimate)   # least negative
lolo_max_est <- min(lolo_tbl$estimate)   # most negative
lolo_worst   <- lolo_tbl %>% slice_max(p, n = 1)

# Leave-one-category-out: the language jackknife retains nearly every
# unilemma on each pass (the shape predictor is unilemma-level), so also
# drop each semantic category, which removes its unilemmas entirely.
loco_cats <- sort(unique(predictors_df_few$category))
loco_tbl <- purrr::map_dfr(loco_cats, function(cc) {
  d   <- predictors_df_few %>% filter(category != cc)
  fit <- suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(lmerTest::lmer(
    aoa ~ logfreq + concreteness + solid + mean_shape + count_noun + language +
          (1 | category) + (1 | uni_lemma),
    data = d)))
  cf <- coef(summary(fit))["mean_shape", ]
  tibble::tibble(
    dropped_category = cc,
    estimate = cf[["Estimate"]],
    p        = cf[["Pr(>|t|)"]])
})
loco_n_sig   <- sum(loco_tbl$p < .05)
loco_min_est <- max(loco_tbl$estimate)   # least negative
loco_max_est <- min(loco_tbl$estimate)   # most negative
loco_worst   <- loco_tbl %>% slice_max(p, n = 2) %>% arrange(desc(p)) %>%
  mutate(dropped_category = gsub("_", " ", dropped_category))
```

```{r aoa-contrasts}
# Gelman-Stern check: shape significant while solidity/count are not does
# not itself establish that the coefficients differ. Because the predictors
# are z-scored, contrast the coefficients directly, using the fitted
# model's fixed-effect covariance matrix (z test, as in multcomp::glht).
fe_vcov <- as.matrix(vcov(full_fit))
coef_contrast <- function(a, b) {
  d  <- full_coefs[a, "Estimate"] - full_coefs[b, "Estimate"]
  se <- sqrt(fe_vcov[a, a] + fe_vcov[b, b] - 2 * fe_vcov[a, b])
  list(diff = d, se = se, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(d / se)))
}
shape_vs_solid <- coef_contrast("mean_shape", "solid")
shape_vs_count <- coef_contrast("mean_shape", "count_noun")
fmt_contrast <- function(ct) {
  sprintf("difference = %s, $SE$ = %s, %s",
          papaja::printnum(ct$diff, digits = 2),
          papaja::printnum(ct$se, digits = 2),
          fmt_p(ct$p))
}
```

```{r aoa-bayes-power}
# Bayesian refit and single-language power analysis, precomputed by
# analysis/aoa-power-bayes.R (re-run that script before knitting after any
# data update; it writes the two CSVs read here).
bp_power <- read_csv(here("data/predictors", "aoa_power_sensitivity.csv"),
                     show_col_types = FALSE)
bp_bayes <- read_csv(here("data/predictors", "aoa_bayes_summary.csv"),
                     show_col_types = FALSE)

# Simulated power of the English-only design at the pooled slope (first row
# of the simulation grid), and analytic 80%-power minimal detectable effects.
pw_sim_pooled <- bp_power %>%
  filter(design == "English (American) only") %>%
  slice(1) %>% pull(power)
mde_eng_80 <- bp_power %>%
  filter(design == "English-only analytic MDE (80% power)") %>%
  pull(true_shape_slope) %>% abs()
mde_kor_80 <- bp_power %>%
  filter(design == "Korean-predictor analytic MDE (80% power)") %>%
  pull(true_shape_slope) %>% abs()
mde_ratio <- mde_eng_80 / abs(full_coefs["mean_shape", "Estimate"])

# Analytic power of the top-quartile-excluded refit at the pooled slope.
pw_quartile <- pnorm(abs(full_coefs["mean_shape", "Estimate"]) /
                       excl_quartile$coefs["mean_shape", "Std. Error"] -
                       qnorm(.975))

bayes_primary <- bp_bayes %>% filter(model == "cross-linguistic (primary)")
bayes_engrow  <- bp_bayes %>% filter(model == "English (American) only")
```

```{r aoa-aux}
# AT feedback: are more frequent words also more shape-organized?
# Computed at the unilemma level: mean_shape is constant within unilemma, so
# item-by-language rows are not independent units for this CI. Frequency is
# averaged across languages within unilemma.
freq_shape_uni <- ratings_aoa %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(logfreq), !is.na(mean_shape)) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(uni_lemma) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(logfreq = mean(logfreq),
                   mean_shape = dplyr::first(mean_shape), .groups = "drop")
freq_shape_ct  <- cor.test(freq_shape_uni$logfreq, freq_shape_uni$mean_shape)
freq_shape_cor <- as.numeric(freq_shape_ct$estimate)
n_freq_shape   <- nrow(freq_shape_uni)

# Shared variance between concreteness and the solidity/count predictors
# (named in the concreteness range-restriction sentence).
r_conc_solid <- cor(ratings_aoa$concreteness, ratings_aoa$solid,
                    use = "pairwise.complete.obs") %>% as.numeric()
r_conc_count <- cor(ratings_aoa$concreteness, ratings_aoa$count_noun,
                    use = "pairwise.complete.obs") %>% as.numeric()

# Qualitative example words for the "shape vs solidity" dissociation.
# Filter on the *unscaled* ratings_aoa data (not z-scored predictors_df_few).
# Restrict to unilemmas with actual solidity trials: the ratings_aoa build
# zero-fills `solid` for the few nouns absent from the solidity block (e.g.
# trolley), and a filled 0.00 would otherwise surface as an extreme example.
solidity_rated_uni <- english_sample1 %>%
  dplyr::filter(block == "solidity") %>%
  dplyr::distinct(word) %>% dplyr::pull(word)
solid_late_examples <- ratings_aoa %>%
  filter(!is.na(aoa), !is.na(solid), !is.na(mean_shape),
         uni_lemma %in% solidity_rated_uni) %>%
  filter(solid > 0.7, mean_shape < 0.3) %>%
  group_by(uni_lemma) %>%
  summarise(aoa = mean(aoa, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(aoa)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  pull(uni_lemma)

shape_early_examples <- ratings_aoa %>%
  filter(!is.na(aoa), !is.na(solid), !is.na(mean_shape),
         uni_lemma %in% solidity_rated_uni) %>%
  filter(mean_shape > 0.5, solid < 0.5) %>%
  group_by(uni_lemma) %>%
  summarise(aoa = mean(aoa, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(aoa) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  pull(uni_lemma)
```

```{r korean-aoa-model}
# Matched Korean AoA items. Two models on the same rows:
# Eng predictors + Korean logfreq + Brysbaert concreteness;
# Kor predictors + Korean logfreq only (no concreteness: English norms).
# REML = FALSE so AIC is comparable across non-nested models.
ratings_aoa_korean <- ratings_aoa %>% filter(language == "Korean")

kor_preds <- all_data_wide %>%
  select(uni_lemma, kor1, kor2, response_norm) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = response_norm, values_from = c(kor1, kor2),
              values_fill = 0) %>%
  mutate(
    mean_shape_kor = (kor1_shape + kor2_shape) / 2,
    mean_solid_kor = (kor1_solid + kor2_solid) / 2,
    mean_count_kor = (kor1_count + kor2_count) / 2
  ) %>%
  select(uni_lemma, mean_shape_kor, mean_solid_kor, mean_count_kor)

all_data_wide_kor_model <- ratings_aoa_korean %>%
  left_join(kor_preds, by = "uni_lemma") %>%
  # `freq` is already a within-language z-scored log relative frequency
  # (see analysis/build-ratings-aoa.R), so it is not logged again here.
  filter(!is.na(aoa), !is.na(freq)) %>%
  mutate(logfreq = freq) %>%
  drop_na(concreteness, solid, mean_shape, count_noun,
          mean_shape_kor, mean_solid_kor, mean_count_kor, category) %>%
  distinct(uni_lemma, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(across(
    c(logfreq, concreteness, solid, mean_shape, count_noun,
      mean_solid_kor, mean_shape_kor, mean_count_kor),
    ~ as.numeric(scale(.x))
  ))

korean_aoa_n <- nrow(all_data_wide_kor_model)
kor_lmer_ctrl <- lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa",
                             optCtrl = list(maxfun = 2e5))

korean_eng_fit <- lmerTest::lmer(
  aoa ~ logfreq + concreteness + solid + mean_shape + count_noun +
        (1 | category),
  data = all_data_wide_kor_model, REML = FALSE, control = kor_lmer_ctrl)
korean_eng_coefs <- coef(summary(korean_eng_fit))

korean_fit <- lmerTest::lmer(
  aoa ~ logfreq + mean_solid_kor + mean_shape_kor + mean_count_kor +
        (1 | category),
  data = all_data_wide_kor_model, REML = FALSE, control = kor_lmer_ctrl)
korean_coefs <- coef(summary(korean_fit))

korean_aic <- c(
  eng = AIC(korean_eng_fit),
  kor = AIC(korean_fit)
)

korean_r2 <- if (requireNamespace("MuMIn", quietly = TRUE)) {
  list(
    eng = as.numeric(MuMIn::r.squaredGLMM(korean_eng_fit)[1, "R2m"]),
    kor = as.numeric(MuMIn::r.squaredGLMM(korean_fit)[1, "R2m"])
  )
} else {
  list(eng = NA_real_, kor = NA_real_)
}
```

In the cross-linguistic unilemma mixed-effects model (Table \@ref(tab:aoa-table)), frequency was the strongest predictor (`r fmt_coef(full_coefs, "logfreq")`), with more frequent words acquired `r papaja::printnum(full_coefs["logfreq", "Estimate"], digits = 2)` months earlier per SD, while concreteness added nothing (`r fmt_coef(full_coefs, "concreteness")`), which is expected to be range-restricted in this item set of early nouns. The mean shape rating remained a significant unique predictor of AoA above and beyond these covariates (`r fmt_coef(full_coefs, "mean_shape")`, 95% Wald CI [`r papaja::printnum(shape_wald_ci[1], digits = 2)`, `r papaja::printnum(shape_wald_ci[2], digits = 2)`]), with higher shape ratings associated with `r papaja::printnum(full_coefs["mean_shape", "Estimate"], digits = 2)` months earlier acquisition per SD, comparable to the range of reliable item-level AoA predictors in this literature [@tan2024predicting]. Solidity (`r fmt_coef(full_coefs, "solid")`) and count-noun status (`r fmt_coef(full_coefs, "count_noun")`) were not reliably different from zero. Adding a per-language random slope left the fixed effect unchanged (`r fmt_coef(slope_coefs, "mean_shape")`). Contrasting the z-scored coefficients directly, shape's coefficient was reliably more negative than solidity's (`r fmt_contrast(shape_vs_solid)`), while its difference from count-noun status was not reliable (`r fmt_contrast(shape_vs_count)`) [@gelman_stern_2006]. Shape thus predicts AoA at least as well as properties that are far more common in the early lexicon. 
A Bayesian refit of the same model with weakly informative priors (normal(0, 5) on the coefficients) gives a posterior for the shape coefficient with `r papaja::printnum(100 * bayes_primary$p_negative, digits = 1)`% of its mass below zero (mean = `r papaja::printnum(bayes_primary$post_mean, digits = 2)`, 95% CrI [`r papaja::printnum(bayes_primary$ci_low, digits = 2)`, `r papaja::printnum(bayes_primary$ci_high, digits = 2)`]); the full posterior summary is in Supplement S9.  
Refitting after excluding the most widely shared unilemmas (unilemmas appearing in more than `r excl_decile$thr` of the `r length(unique(predictors_df_few$language))` language sets) preserved the effect (`r fmt_coef(excl_decile$coefs, "mean_shape")`; `r excl_decile$n_uni` unilemmas). Refitting the model `r nrow(lolo_tbl)` times, dropping one language's items on each pass, left the shape coefficient negative and reliable in every one, within a narrow band (`r papaja::printnum(lolo_max_est, digits = 2)` to `r papaja::printnum(lolo_min_est, digits = 2)`, against a pooled estimate of `r papaja::printnum(full_coefs["mean_shape", "Estimate"], digits = 2)`; weakest when `r lolo_worst$dropped_language` was dropped, `r papaja::printnum(lolo_worst$estimate, digits = 2)`, `r fmt_p(lolo_worst$p)`), so no single language carries the association (Supplement S8). 
The artifact-only sensitivity model, refit after excluding semantic categories (animals, body parts, clothing, outside) whose acquisition trajectories may not be governed by the same processes, preserved the pattern and shape remained a significant predictor (`r fmt_coef(artifact_coefs, "mean_shape")`). Because solidity and count-noun status come from the initial Study 1 sample alone while shape averages two samples, we also refit the model with the initial-sample shape proportion in place of the average, so all three lexical predictors come from a single sample with comparable split-half reliabilities (`r sb_solid_1a`, `r sb_count_1a`, and `r sb_shape_1a`, respectively); shape remained a reliable predictor (`r fmt_coef(s1only_coefs, "shape_s1")`).

```{r aoa-table, include=FALSE}
focal_terms <- c("(Intercept)", "logfreq", "concreteness",
                 "solid", "mean_shape", "count_noun")
focal_terms <- focal_terms[focal_terms %in% rownames(full_coefs)]

aoa_table_df <- tibble::tibble(
  Predictor   = dplyr::recode(focal_terms,
                              `(Intercept)` = "Intercept",
                              `logfreq`     = "Log frequency",
                              `concreteness` = "Concreteness",
                              `solid`       = "Solidity",
                              `mean_shape`  = "Mean shape",
                              `count_noun`  = "Count-noun"),
  Estimate    = papaja::printnum(full_coefs[focal_terms, "Estimate"],   digits = 2),
  SE          = papaja::printnum(full_coefs[focal_terms, "Std. Error"], digits = 2),
  df          = papaja::printnum(full_coefs[focal_terms, "df"],         digits = 1),
  `t value`   = papaja::printnum(full_coefs[focal_terms, "t value"],    digits = 2),
  p           = papaja::printp(full_coefs[focal_terms, "Pr(>|t|)"]))
```

A model fit to the English (American) items alone ($N$ = `r nrow(engonly_df)`) reproduced the association (`r fmt_coef(engonly_coefs, "mean_shape")`). On the matched Korean AoA item set ($N$ = `r korean_aoa_n`), the English-predictor model recovered only frequency (`r fmt_coef(korean_eng_coefs, "logfreq")`). In the Korean-predictor model, countability status showed a unique association (`r fmt_coef(korean_coefs, "mean_count_kor")`, more countable-like items acquired earlier), while more solid items acquired later (`r fmt_coef(korean_coefs, "mean_solid_kor")`), and shape was not reliable (`r fmt_coef(korean_coefs, "mean_shape_kor")`). Comparing the two, the Korean-predictor model fits slightly better (AIC `r papaja::printnum(korean_aic["kor"], digits = 1)` vs. `r papaja::printnum(korean_aic["eng"], digits = 1)`; marginal $R^2$ `r papaja::printnum(korean_r2$kor, digits = 2)` vs. `r papaja::printnum(korean_r2$eng, digits = 2)`) and supplies a different signal (countability status).
Simulating the English-only design at its current size recovers an effect of the pooled magnitude `r papaja::printnum(100 * pw_sim_pooled, digits = 0)`% of the time, and the Korean-predictor model is even smaller. We therefore read the absence of a Korean shape effect as uninformative rather than as contradicting the pooled unilemma fit. 

Since items entered the study because they are early-acquired, it by design truncates the outcome's range, which likely attenuates the slopes relative to what an unrestricted vocabulary would show. The shape-AoA association is therefore established for early-acquired nouns specifically; whether it extends across the full vocabulary is a question this design cannot answer.

One possibility could be that frequent words are also more shape-organized, which would imply that the shape effect on AoA is partly redundant with frequency. Across our items, the correlation between log frequency and mean shape rating is essentially zero ($r$ = `r papaja::printnum(freq_shape_cor, digits = 3)`, 95% CI [`r papaja::printnum(freq_shape_ct$conf.int[1], digits = 2)`, `r papaja::printnum(freq_shape_ct$conf.int[2], digits = 2)`], $N$ = `r prettyNum(n_freq_shape, big.mark = ",")` unilemmas; computed at the unilemma level), indicating that frequency and shape-organization carry independent information about which words are acquired early. 

```{r aoa-reverse-causality, include=FALSE}
# Reverse-causality check: refit the primary model adding adult norms that
# index the "familiar early word" pathway. Full analysis (coverage, added
# coefficients, range restriction) in writeup/reverse-causality.Rmd; norm
# files live in data/predictors/external/.
clean_lemma <- function(x) {
  x %>% str_to_lower() %>% str_remove("\\s*\\(.*\\)\\s*$") %>%
    str_split_fixed("/", 2) %>% .[, 1] %>% str_trim()
}
kuperman_norms <- readxl::read_xlsx(here("data/predictors/external",
                                         "kuperman_aoa_with_pos.xlsx")) %>%
  janitor::clean_names() %>%
  transmute(match_word = str_to_lower(word),
            adult_aoa  = as.numeric(rating_mean)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(adult_aoa)) %>%
  distinct(match_word, .keep_all = TRUE)
glasgow_norms <- read_csv(here("data/predictors/external", "glasgow_norms.csv"),
                          show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  janitor::clean_names() %>%
  transmute(match_word   = clean_lemma(word),
            imageability = as.numeric(m_imag),
            familiarity  = as.numeric(m_fam)) %>%
  group_by(match_word) %>%
  summarise(across(c(imageability, familiarity), mean), .groups = "drop")
braginsky_norms <- read_csv(here("data/predictors/external",
                                 "braginsky_uni_predictors.csv"),
                            show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  filter(language == "English (American)") %>%
  transmute(match_word = clean_lemma(uni_lemma), babiness, valence, arousal) %>%
  distinct(match_word, .keep_all = TRUE)
rc_df <- ratings_aoa %>%
  mutate(match_word = clean_lemma(uni_lemma)) %>%
  left_join(kuperman_norms,  by = "match_word") %>%
  left_join(glasgow_norms,   by = "match_word") %>%
  left_join(braginsky_norms, by = "match_word") %>%
  distinct(language, uni_lemma, .keep_all = TRUE)
rc_fit <- function(extra) {
  covs <- c("logfreq", "concreteness", "solid", "mean_shape", "count_noun",
            extra)
  d <- rc_df %>%
    select(uni_lemma, aoa, category, language, all_of(covs)) %>%
    drop_na() %>%
    mutate(across(all_of(covs), ~ as.numeric(scale(.x)))) %>%
    distinct()
  fit <- lmerTest::lmer(
    reformulate(c(covs, "language", "(1 | category)", "(1 | uni_lemma)"),
                response = "aoa"),
    data = d)
  list(coefs = coef(summary(fit)), n_uni = dplyr::n_distinct(d$uni_lemma))
}
rc_imgfam <- rc_fit(c("imageability", "familiarity"))
rc_adult  <- rc_fit("adult_aoa")
rc_all    <- rc_fit(c("imageability", "familiarity", "adult_aoa",
                      "babiness", "valence", "arousal"))
```

A related alternative is that adults may judge familiar, early, highly imageable words to be shape-organized, rather than shape organization tracking acquisition creating a reverse causality. Testing this left the shape coefficient intact: `r fmt_coef(rc_imgfam$coefs, "mean_shape")` with adult imageability and familiarity added [Glasgow Norms, `r rc_imgfam$n_uni` matched unilemmas; @scott2019], `r fmt_coef(rc_adult$coefs, "mean_shape")` with adult English AoA added [`r rc_adult$n_uni` unilemmas; @kuperman2012], and `r fmt_coef(rc_all$coefs, "mean_shape")` with all six adult covariates entered together (adding babiness, valence, and arousal). These fits do not identify the causal direction, but they are inconsistent with the shape rating merely proxying the adult accessibility of early words.

```{r qualitative-dissociation-table, include=FALSE}
qual_late <- ratings_aoa %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(aoa), !is.na(solid), !is.na(mean_shape),
                uni_lemma %in% solidity_rated_uni,
                solid > 0.7, mean_shape < 0.3) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(uni_lemma) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(Shape = mean(mean_shape), Solidity = mean(solid),
                   AoA = mean(aoa), .groups = "drop") %>%
  dplyr::arrange(desc(AoA)) %>% dplyr::slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(grp = "late")

qual_early <- ratings_aoa %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(aoa), !is.na(solid), !is.na(mean_shape),
                uni_lemma %in% solidity_rated_uni,
                mean_shape > 0.5, solid < 0.5) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(uni_lemma) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(Shape = mean(mean_shape), Solidity = mean(solid),
                   AoA = mean(aoa), .groups = "drop") %>%
  dplyr::arrange(AoA) %>% dplyr::slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(grp = "early")

qual_tab <- dplyr::bind_rows(qual_early, qual_late)
qual_tab_display <- tibble::tibble(
  Noun        = qual_tab$uni_lemma,
  Shape       = papaja::printnum(qual_tab$Shape,    digits = 2),
  Solidity    = papaja::printnum(qual_tab$Solidity, digits = 2),
  `AoA (mo.)` = papaja::printnum(qual_tab$AoA,      digits = 1)
)

qual_stub_indents <- list(
  "High shape, low solidity (acquired early)" =
    which(qual_tab$grp == "early"),
  "High solidity, low shape (acquired late)" =
    which(qual_tab$grp == "late")
)
```

\input{tables_pair_b.tex}

**Qualitative examples.** Table \@ref(tab:qualitative-dissociation-table) contrasts two profiles of nouns. Nouns rated highly solid but low on shape, such as `r paste(qual_late$uni_lemma[1:3], collapse = ", ")`, are acquired late and are typically larger, more complex, or less canonically shaped artifacts. Nouns with a clear shared shape but lower solidity, such as `r paste(qual_early$uni_lemma[1:3], collapse = ", ")`, are acquired comparatively early despite their less prototypical "object-ness." Being solid is no guarantee that a category has a shared shape, and these cases show that a clear shape signal can scaffold word acquisition even when other lexical correlates are weak.

# General Discussion

This work tested the statistical generalization account of the shape bias by measuring the distributional dominance of shape in the early lexicon and asking (i) whether those lexical statistics explain cross-linguistic variation in the shape bias, and (ii) whether they predict the age at which individual words are learned. Our results converge on a single framing: shape is a good cue for early noun learning, but it is not ubiquitous i.e. few early nouns name categories that adults judge to be organized by shape, but the nouns that do, are learned earlier. Across five English and Korean samples, shape-organized categories were considerably less dominant in the early lexicon than previously expected, yet, shape predicted age of acquisition. The features that predict early word learning are therefore not the same as the features that are common in early word learning. This dissociation is hard to reconcile with a pure exposure account, on which the shape bias is a downstream consequence of how often shape-organized count nouns appear in the input. It is more easily reconciled with a learnability account, on which the presence of a clear shape signal in a category makes that category easier to learn, when it happens to be there.

## Korean adult ratings exceed English: a puzzle for the simplest statistical account

The Korean data shows a pattern that is opposite of what the simplest version of the statistical-generalization account predicts: if cross-linguistic variation in the child shape bias were a downstream consequence of cross-linguistic variation in the lexical statistics adults perceive, we should have found fewer shape-organized nouns in Korean compared to English. We see at least three candidate explanations:

1. The Korean classifier system directs adult attention to shape. Korean lacks the count-mass syntax of English but obligatorily uses numeral classifiers when counting, and choosing one requires the speaker to settle what kind of thing, and in which form, the referent is: "myeong" for people, "mari" for animals, "gae" as the general classifier for inanimate objects, "jaru" for long thin implements such as pens, "jang" for flat sheet-like things such as paper, and "al" for small round things such as eggs [@sohn_1999; see also @allan_1977; @aikhenvald_2000]. A lifetime of this counting may raise the salience of shape and made it highly codable when adults are asked to reflect on it explicitly, especially in ambiguous contexts [@speed2021classifier], without making shape the cue toddlers weight most in the moment extension task. Chinese-speaking adults, whose classifier system encodes shape in a similar way, relied on shape more than English speakers in object classification tasks, grouping a snake with a rope [@kuo_sera_2009], although classifier effects on similarity judgments are reported to be small relative to shared taxonomic and thematic structure [@saalbach_imai_2007]. This account locates the difference in adult linguistic experience rather than in the input available to toddlers, which fits our scoping of adult ratings as an index of the learned lexicon. It also generates a testable prediction that adult speakers of other numeral-classifier languages whose classifiers encode shape should show similarly elevated shape ratings under the matched forced-choice procedure.

2. Adult raters can attend to articulable features ("a knife has a typical shape") that toddlers may not weight in the same way during word learning. The adult lexical-statistics measure is not a direct measure of child input; it is a measure of what adults notice in retrospect.

3. The in-country sample was recruited locally, while the online sample may have consisted largely of bilingual Koreans living abroad. The fact that the higher shape rating replicates across these two samples argues against a pure language-of-residence effect, but a residual sample-location, cultural, or recruitment confound cannot be ruled out.

Within each block, English and Korean item-level means were positively correlated. The puzzle is therefore not that Korean and English raters disagree on every dimension, or on which nouns are more shape-organized than others, but about the absolute shape-organization ratings. 

## Linguistic statistics versus environmental statistics

The statistical-generalization account could partially be about children's environments, but our results, and our methodology, speak only to the learned lexicon, not to the visual or referential environment. In principle the two could decouple. Children across the world live among broadly similar inventories of shape-coherent artifacts and natural kinds, but the language they are learning may direct attention to different subsets of those objects, and may mark different organizing features as relevant [@majid_etal_2004; @levinson_2003]. Anthropological and cross-cultural work documenting variation in the kinds and salience of artifacts and natural kinds in less industrialized societies [@brown_1998; @jara2022] suggests environmental statistics could partially explain the word extension task results. Disentangling lexical from environmental statistics in the same children would require ecological measurements of object exposure (e.g., from headcam corpora) alongside vocabulary, which is a clear next step for this line of work.

## Limitations and future directions

First, the shape-AoA result rests on English-rater predictors. It holds in the pooled model and in the English-only fit, but the Korean-rater models are a weaker test: the power analysis in Study 4 indicates that a within-language design of that size detects only slopes about `r papaja::printnum(mde_kor_80 / abs(full_coefs["mean_shape", "Estimate"]), digits = 1)` times our pooled estimate. We report them so the cross-linguistic claim is not mistaken for a within-Korean one, a replication the current Korean item set is underpowered to deliver.

Second, our adult-rating approach captures the cumulative version of the shape bias (which features characterize the early lexicon) rather than the in-the-moment version (which features children rely on when extending a novel label). Linking the two will require measuring lexical statistics and children's generalization behavior in the same languages; a direct per-language regression on child effect sizes is not yet possible, since the literature supplies too few non-English language-level estimates [@Abdelrahim_Frank_2026]. 
Third, our cross-linguistic isolates the conceptual mappings lexicon-side prediction but it cannot detect cases where two language communities conceptualize the same item differently. Study 2 partly addresses this, but extension to typologically diverse non-Indo-European languages is needed. 

Fourth, our conditional analyses engage the overhypothesis version of the statistical-generalization account [@kemp_learning_2007] only descriptively. On that version, children learn a second-order generalization over solid, count nouns, so the relevant statistic is the coherence of the solid-count-shape cluster rather than the marginal share of shape-organized nouns. That intersection is sparse in our data, which suggests the early lexicon offers this generalization less support than earlier counts implied. A hierarchical model that estimates the strength of the overhypothesis directly from these ratings is a next test, along with within-category visual variability as an additional cue. 

Fifth, we relied on Wordbank-derived AoA estimates as our outcome measure in Study 4; while this is a standard external-validation strategy, it inherits the assumptions of the parental-report instruments used in different languages. Lastly, the procedure-dependence of the shape statistic, documented in Study 3, carries a general methodological lesson for this literature. The randomized experiment showed that the reported level of shape organization is governed first by the analyst's coding rule and second by whether items are grouped by semantic category.

## Conclusion

The shape bias remains a robust phenomenon in early noun learning. What our results call into question is the simplest version of the statistical generalization explanation for it. The lexical statistics that ground this account turn out to be less dominant in early lexicons than was previously thought, and their apparent dominance depends in part on how they are measured; they appear stable across the English-rated unilemma sets of typologically diverse languages, a design that cannot detect conceptual differences between language communities; and where they do vary across rater groups, they vary in a direction opposite to what the cross-linguistic developmental literature would predict. At the same time, shape reliably predicted acquisition at least as well as the features that dominate the lexical statistics we measured. Together, these findings reposition the shape bias as a learnability bias more than an exposure bias: shape is a useful cue when it is available, not a feature children come to expect because it is everywhere.
